Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html

# Let Clio Coder work without watching every call

> Check the sandbox, undo a change with /rewind, tell the safety judge about your machine, and know when yolo is the right call.

Most of a coding task should not need you. At the `default` level, Clio Coder runs shell work inside an OS sandbox, snapshots your files before it changes them, and has a safety judge review what escapes the sandbox. You are asked only when the judge has no verdict or the decision is yours.

This guide shows how to check that setup, undo a change, and choose when to step up to `yolo`.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. The sandbox needs bubblewrap on Linux; on macOS it uses an experimental `sandbox-exec` profile. Snapshots need a Git work tree. Native Windows has neither guarantee, so read what `doctor` reports on your host.

## Before you start

- Clio Coder installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository you can experiment in, with a clean working tree.

### Check what this host can contain

```sh
clio-coder doctor
```

Look for the `shell sandbox` row. It names the backend and where contained commands may write. If no backend exists, commands outside the recognized set go to the judge and then to you, so the rest of this guide still holds with more questions.

### Give it a task and watch what happens

On a scratch branch, type this:

```text
Delete the build output directory, regenerate it, and run the project's test check. Report what you ran.
```

Workspace edits and contained commands run without a card. A delete inside the workspace runs after a snapshot, because the snapshot can undo it. A push or a command that leaves the sandbox goes to the judge first.

### Undo it with /rewind

```text
/rewind
```

The list shows this session's snapshots, newest first, with how many files each differs by. `Enter` previews a restore before anything is written. Confirming takes one more snapshot, so the rewind itself can be rewound.

### Tell the judge about your machine

The judge reads your typed messages and the proposed call. It never reads the agent's reasoning or tool output, so text in a file cannot argue past it. Name what is yours in your user settings:

```yaml title=settings.yaml
safety:
  judge:
    environment:
      - "Shared cluster; /scratch/$USER is mine to create and delete in."
    allow:
      - "restarting the dev containers this project's compose file defines"
```

**What you should see**

Contained work runs without a card, and `/rewind` lists a snapshot from before the first change of the turn. This shows the controls work on your host. It does not show that the agent's change is correct, so review the diff and the check results.

## What still reaches you

Some decisions never go to the judge: `ask_user` questions, Clio Coder's own settings, a plan-scale dispatch, and a model edit of project settings. A permission card nobody answers within `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) is denied, never approved, and the turn continues. A question nobody answers takes its recommended option, and `/decisions` shows what was chosen for you.

## When to use yolo

`yolo` is a skip-permissions mode for long jobs in a container or another disposable environment. Nothing asks, and commands run unsandboxed with your credentials.

```sh
clio-coder --autonomy yolo
```

The first interactive activation shows a one-time acceptance card, and yolo is refused as root outside a detected container. A short floor still blocks deleting your home directory or a system tree, `mkfs`, writes to a block device, fork bombs, and reads of Clio Coder's credential store. Your project's approved rules and the run's ceilings also hold. Snapshots stay on.

| | `default` | `yolo` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shell commands | In the OS sandbox when a backend exists | Unsandboxed as you |
| Would-be approvals | Judge first, then you | None |
| Your questions | Wait, then resolve after the timeout | Answered at once |
| Workers | Own sandbox, asks go to the judge | Own sandbox, run the yolo way in their scope |
| `/rewind` | Available | Available |

**What this does not protect**

- The sandbox contains `bash` and `run_script`. Typed `write` and `edit` calls follow the rules instead.
- Ignored files, untracked files over 16 MiB, and nested repositories are not in a snapshot.
- `/rewind` restores files. It never moves refs: it prints the commands that bring a moved branch back.
- The judge is a model. It can be wrong, and a route error means no verdict, so the call parks or is denied.
- Stronger isolation needs an external sandbox such as a container.

**Next steps**

- [Tools and permissions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-a-playbook-and-land-it.html

# Run a playbook and land the result

> Run the builtin sdlc playbook on one task, watch it work, and land the branch it keeps after you preview the change.

A playbook is a sequence of workers and code steps that the fleet runs for you. The builtin `sdlc` playbook plans, builds, tests with a bounded fix loop, reviews with a bounded revise loop, and documents, with three commits along the way. This guide runs it on one task and lands the result on your branch.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. `fleet land` needs Git 2.38 or newer. Run time and cost depend on your repository and the model you connect, so start with a small task.

## Before you start

- Clio Coder installed, with a connected model that supports tool calling.
- A clean Git repository with a test command.
- A small, specific task you could review by hand.

### See what is available

```sh
clio-coder playbook list
```

`sdlc` shows as `setup` until the project declares the two commands it runs, `test` and `commit`.

### Declare the commands it runs

```sh
clio-coder playbook commands init
```

This drafts `.clio-coder/playbooks/commands.yaml` from your project's declarations, fully commented out, because uncommenting an entry confirms its exact command. Edit it to name what this project runs:

```yaml title=.clio-coder/playbooks/commands.yaml
version: 1
commands:
  test:
    argv: ["npm", "run", "test"]
  commit:
    argv: ["git", "commit", "-m", "{{commitMessage}}"]
```

### Check before you run

```sh
clio-coder playbook validate sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
clio-coder playbook graph sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
```

`validate` runs the execution preflight and `graph` prints the compiled waves, loops, scopes, and write boundaries, both without side effects. It resolves agents, targets, and profiles, and checks the session budget and write boundaries. A failed preflight during a real run exits 2 before anything dispatches.

### Run it

```sh
clio-coder fleet run sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
```

The first line names the fleet root and plan hash. Each settled step prints one line. In another terminal, `clio-coder fleet status` shows the board and `clio-coder fleet events <root>` follows the journal.

### Land what it kept

```sh
clio-coder fleet land
clio-coder fleet land <run id>
clio-coder fleet land <run id> --yes --plan <id>
```

The first command lists the task branches finished runs kept. The second previews one: commits, changes, destination, whether it fast-forwards, and any conflict. It changes nothing. The third lands exactly that preview. Add `--squash` for one commit instead of the history.

![Terminal output: playbook validate sdlc reports 8 declared steps, 6 code steps, 4 agents and 14 plan steps; playbook graph lists waves 1 to 14 with each step's kind, agent or command, and scope, then the suite and review loops.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-playbook-graph.webp)

*Validate and graph print the compiled plan for the built-in sdlc playbook without running a step.*

**What you should see**

A summary with each loop's terminal reason and any steps that need your decision, then commits on your branch after you land. A finished run shows the playbook ran and its checks passed. It does not show the change is right, so read the diff.

## Make it yours

```sh
clio-coder playbook new parser-fix --from sdlc
```

This copies the builtin to `.clio-coder/playbooks/parser-fix.md`, where you can change steps, agents, and limits. A resumed run replays a completed prefix of the same plan: `clio-coder fleet run <name> --resume <runId>`.

**Boundaries**

- Under `fleet run` nobody is attached, so a worker's ordinary ask is denied, not judged.
- One lock per Git checkout keeps two fleets out of the same workspace.
- `clio-coder telemetry verify --run <run-id>` checks the record of a run. The journals are hash-chained and unsigned, so they show consistency, not who wrote them.

**Next steps**

- [Workers and fleets](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html

# Run it unattended within limits

> Start a headless run with a cost ceiling and a timeout, ask read-only questions, schedule turns, and know what stops each one.

You can start a task and leave. Headless `clio-coder run` does one turn with nobody attached, and the limits you set are enforced. This guide covers a bounded headless run, a read-only one, the timeouts that apply when you walk away from an open session, and scheduled turns.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. A headless run has no one to ask: it denies whatever the safety judge does not allow, and `ask_user` is not available.

## Before you start

- Clio Coder installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository, and a task you can state completely in one prompt.

### Put your decisions in the prompt

The judge reads only your prompt in a headless run, so name the actions the job needs:

```sh
clio-coder run --max-cost-usd 2 --timeout 1800 \
  "Fix the failing parser test, run the test check, and commit on this branch. Do not push."
```

`--max-cost-usd` caps the priced spend this run adds. Reaching it stops the run and its workers with exit 4 and `budget_ceiling`. Calls already in flight can pass the cap, and unpriced routes cannot be bounded, so pair it with `--timeout`, which exits 124 on expiry. The session ceiling, 5 USD by default, still applies.

### Ask a question that cannot change anything

```sh
clio-coder run --read-only "Which modules have no tests? Report paths."
```

`--read-only` is an enforced ceiling on the main agent, not a request. It denies calls other than reads inside the workspace.

### Stream it to another program

```sh
clio-coder run --json "Summarize the last five commits."
```

The stream opens with a `session` header carrying its schema version, and a run that fails before any output still ends with a `turn_end` frame. Continue later with `--continue` or `--session <id prefix>`.

### Walk away from an open session

In the terminal, an unanswered permission card is denied after `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) and the turn continues. A question takes its recommended option. Any key stops the countdown. When you return, `/decisions` shows what was chosen, and the exit summary counts it on an `Unattended` line.

### Schedule turns while idle

```text
/loop 30m Check the nightly build log and report anything new.
/loop 5m --command make check
/loop list
```

A loop runs only while its conversation is idle and never replays missed runs. The `--command` form polls a program directly, with no shell.

**What you should see**

A finished turn with its exit code, not a parked prompt. An exit of 4 means the cost ceiling stopped it. `clio-coder telemetry why-stopped <session>` explains a stop afterward.

| When you want | Use | What still stops it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One bounded task | `clio-coder run` at `default` | Judge, sandbox, cost ceiling, timeout |
| A long job in a container | `clio-coder run --autonomy yolo` | The floor, your rules, ceilings, the loop guard, the tool budget |
| A recurring check | `/loop` in an open session | Pause or stop it; needs the session to stay open |

**Boundaries**

- A contained command starts without credential variables and cannot open secret files, so name tools that need them. Clio Coder may rerun with `unsandboxed: true`, which the judge reviews.
- `yolo` does not carry over from `settings.yaml` to a headless run. It comes only from that run's own `--autonomy yolo`, and it exits 2 as root outside a detected container.

**Next steps**

- [Let Clio Coder work without watching every call](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html

# See what a session cost and what a run did

> Read session cost and stop reasons from local journals, verify a sealed record, and prepare an archive that uploads nothing.

Clio Coder records what each process, session, and worker run did in local journals, and every usage figure on every surface comes from those journals. This guide shows how to read a session's cost, find out why it stopped, check a run's record, and prepare an archive for a maintainer.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. Costs are shown with their provenance: a measured figure, an estimate, and an unknown value stay separate. An unknown stays unknown rather than becoming zero.

## Before you start

- Clio Coder installed, and at least one finished session in a repository.
- The session id, which the exit summary prints. `/resume` also lists them.

### Read it in the session

```text
/usage
/context
/health
```

`/usage` covers session usage and supported subscription quotas. `/context` shows context use and the newest call's cache evidence. `/health` shows process health and route state.

### Read it from the shell

```sh
clio-coder telemetry inspect <session>
clio-coder telemetry cost <session> --by model
clio-coder telemetry calls <session> --limit 20
clio-coder telemetry cache <session>
```

Each takes `--json` and returns the same data the terminal, editors, and desktop app read. For a repository over time, use `clio-coder telemetry cost --repo . --days 30 --by model`.

### Ask why it stopped

```sh
clio-coder telemetry why-stopped <session>
clio-coder telemetry timeline <session>
clio-coder telemetry explain <ref>
```

`explain` shows how a figure was derived. `--run <run-id>` points `inspect` and `cost` at one worker run instead of a session.

### Check a record

```sh
clio-coder telemetry verify <session>
clio-coder telemetry verify --run <run-id>
```

A sealed scope directory is self-contained, so you can copy it and verify it on another machine. `verify` checks journal segments, objects, and seals.

### Share it deliberately

```sh
clio-coder telemetry share --session <id> --profile content-free --dry-run
clio-coder telemetry share --session <id> --profile content-free --out report.tar.gz
```

`share` writes an archive and uploads nothing. `content-free` is the default profile, with structural records and no objects or content. `structural` adds objects that hold structure, such as prompt manifests. Read the dry run before you send anything.

![Terminal output: telemetry why-stopped shows a closed session with spend not measured, telemetry verify reports the session sealed with 66 lines in one segment, and telemetry cost by turn shows tokens as lower bounds and cost as not measured.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-telemetry-session.webp)

*A gateway that reports no usage: token figures are lower bounds, cost reads not measured, and the record still verifies.*

**What you should see**

Figures labelled by provenance, and a `verify` result that names any gap. A clean verify shows the journals are internally consistent. The chain is unsigned, so it does not show who wrote them, and it says nothing about whether the work was correct.

## Control what is kept

`telemetry.mode` defaults to `standard`, which keeps accountability and operational records without prompt content. `research` mode, `telemetry.research.content: true`, and `clio-coder telemetry consent` in the workspace are all required before prompts and request bodies are kept.

`clio-coder telemetry prune` is a dry run unless you pass `--apply`.

**Boundaries**

- Figures depend on what the provider reports. Calls with unknown usage are counted separately.
- Quota rows are what a provider account reports, shared across sessions, and are separate from session spend.
- `clio-coder usage report` is experimental.

**Next steps**

- [Run it unattended within limits](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html)
- [Check your installation](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/doctor.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html

# A numerical change, checked with Clio Coder

> Follow a temperature-conversion example through a floating-point test failure, a correction, and recorded verification.

A small numerical task makes it easy to follow a change from code to a recorded check. This example converts temperatures between Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit, validates inputs, and tests physical boundaries without adding dependencies.

## Open the example

Download the [runnable temperature-calibration example](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/temperature-calibration.zip). It includes the actual implementation, seven tests, and a private package manifest. It uses only the built-in Node.js test runner, so it needs `node` and `npm` on your `PATH` and nothing else. The installer's private Node.js is not added to `PATH`.

Extract the archive into your project's `examples/` folder, so the files live in `examples/temperature-calibration/`. Open the project in the terminal:

```sh
clio-coder
```

Select a model that supports tool calling. You can also use the desktop alpha with `clio-coder gui --open`. To reproduce the authoring task in your own project, ask:

> Create four temperature conversion functions for Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit. Reject non-numeric and non-finite inputs with TypeError, and temperatures below absolute zero with RangeError. Use 273.15 for the Celsius/Kelvin offset. Add Node.js tests for freezing, boiling, absolute zero, round trips within 1e-10, and invalid inputs. Use no dependencies. Run the tests and report the actual result.

Choose a new example directory when creating files. In the supplied example, the implementation and tests are already present; start by asking Clio Coder to read them.

## Check the numerical boundaries

These reference temperatures cover ordinary values and the physical lower boundary:

| Reference | Celsius | Kelvin | Fahrenheit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Freezing point | 0 °C | 273.15 K | 32 °F |
| Boiling point | 100 °C | 373.15 K | 212 °F |
| Absolute zero | −273.15 °C | 0 K | −459.67 °F |

When Clio Coder first wrote this example, the first run exposed an exact-equality assertion for the Fahrenheit value at absolute zero. JavaScript produced `−459.66999999999996`; the test expected `−459.67`. Clio changed that assertion to an absolute tolerance of `1e-10` and reran the tests. Review a tolerance against your domain’s numerical requirements before applying it elsewhere.

## Run a declared check

The example’s private `package.json` declares its test command. With the archive extracted into the folder above, ask Clio Coder:

> Use verify with check test and cwd examples/temperature-calibration, then show the reference temperatures from examples/temperature-calibration/calibration.test.mjs as a table. Do not edit files.

Review any permission request before allowing the command. In the recorded run, the check exited 0 with seven passing tests, and Clio read the test file for the table. Naming the file keeps a fast model from searching the project for it.

![Clio Coder in the terminal running the declared test check through verify with exit 0, then showing the reference temperatures from the test file as a table](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/tui-verify.webp)

To run the same tests yourself from the repository root:

```sh
node --test examples/temperature-calibration/calibration.test.mjs
```

## Inspect the recorded result

In the terminal, open `/view` and select the `checked test` row. The preview shows the check, its working directory, the exit status, and the output, so you can compare the answer with what ran. On the desktop alpha, **Artifacts** in the Session column lists the same record.

![Terminal View dock with the transcript list on the left and, on the right, the recorded verify call: check test, its working directory, exit 0, and the passing test lines.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-view-result.webp)

*/view keeps the recorded check, its working directory, and its output.*

Passing tests establish the behavior covered by those tests. This small example does not establish the scientific validity of a larger application. For project-specific requirements, see [quality policies](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html) and [tool usage](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html).

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html

# Choose a model for your project

> Connect a local server, a cloud API, or a supported subscription route, then choose models separately for conversation and delegated work.

Clio Coder lets you choose the model connection around your project. Start with the place your code is allowed to go, then choose a model and runtime that can do the task. A local GPU, a model server, an institutional gateway, and a cloud API are different deployment choices.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. A working connection does not establish a model's coding quality, and routes differ in the tools and images they carry.

## Before you start

- Linux, macOS, or WSL. The installer supplies Node.js.
- A repository you know, so you can judge the first answer.
- One model route you are allowed to use for this code: an app on your computer, a model server, an AI subscription, or a provider account.

## Decide where inference may run

On first setup, Guided setup offers four kinds of route. Choose by where the model input may go, then by what you already run.

| Route | Where inference runs | What the wizard lists |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An app on this computer | Your machine | Ollama, LM Studio, or Lemonade, with a model loaded |
| A model server | The server you name | llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, LiteLLM, or a compatible server |
| An AI subscription | The provider | ChatGPT Plus or Pro, Claude Pro or Max, or an installed Claude tool |
| A provider account or API | The provider | Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, Groq, Mistral, Bedrock, ALCF, or a compatible API |

The wizard shows these providers after you choose the route. A subscription-backed route has its own authentication and usage conditions; it is not interchangeable with an API account. The [connection guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html) covers each route.

**Where each part runs**

1. Clio Coder and its tools (Your computer): The session, repository tools, and approvals run where you start Clio Coder.
2. Inference (The route you choose): A local app, a model server, a subscription, or a provider API. Moves from the previous stage: model requests.
3. Worker tools (Where a worker runs): On this computer by default, or on an SSH node you configure. Moves from the previous stage: delegated work.

*Clio Coder, its tools, and inference can run in different places. Choosing a remote model does not move your files or tools there.*

## Connect one model

### Install Clio Coder

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh
cd /path/to/your/project
```

### Start guided setup

```sh
clio-coder configure
```

Choose **Guided setup**. The desktop alpha offers the same wizard after `clio-coder gui --open`, and `/config` runs it inside a terminal session and applies the result to that session.

### Pick the route and the model

Choose the kind of route, then the app or provider. Confirm the endpoint if it has one, then select a model that supports tool calling. For a local server with no models, load one and choose **Check again**.

### Review the connection, then save

The review shows what setup established. The first connection supplies the chat and worker defaults.

![Guided setup in the terminal asking where the model comes from, with four routes and the providers behind each.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-configure-source.webp)

*Guided setup asks where the model comes from and lists the providers behind each route.*

![Guided setup after choosing Lemonade at 127.0.0.1:13305: the server is reachable and eleven models are listed live.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-configure-models.webp)

*The model list, read live from the local app just now.*

![Guided setup review listing the connection, model, reachable endpoint, eleven live models, and that no generation or tool tests ran, with Save target selected.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-configure-review.webp)

*The review states what Clio Coder could verify and what it did not test.*

Guided setup in the terminal, from the route to the review.

**What you should see**

The model list says whether it is live, cached, or the provider's catalog. Setup checks reachability and the catalog where supported; it does not send a generation request or test tool calling. Reachability is useful, but it is not a coding benchmark.

## Ask one question you can check

**Ask Clio**

> Explain this project's build and test entry points. Do not change files. Identify one check I could run to confirm your explanation.

Read the tool activity and compare the answer with the project. If it fails, check the endpoint, the loaded model, the credentials, and the selected runtime before giving it a larger assignment. `clio-coder doctor` provides diagnostics; it does not certify model quality.

## Separate conversation from worker models

The model answering you need not handle every delegated task. The terminal `/settings` lists the conversation model under **Models & Inference** and worker defaults under **Fleet**; `clio-coder configure --settings` opens the same menu from the shell. On the desktop, Settings has a **Models** page and a **Fleet routes** tab. Select a connection and model for conversation, then use worker defaults or profiles for delegated work.

![Terminal Settings open on Models and Inference, with the chat model, thinking level, and answer length.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-settings-models.webp)

*Settings: the model answering you, under Models and Inference.*

![Terminal Settings open on Fleet, with the default worker connection and model, thinking level, worker location, the local node, and run limits.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-settings-fleet.webp)

*Settings: worker defaults, nodes, and limits under Fleet.*

Terminal settings keep the conversation model and the worker defaults apart.

This helps when exploring a repository and changing code have different requirements, or when you want to keep a workflow while evaluating another model. The benefit depends on the task and environment; this guide makes no claim that a particular combination is cheaper or faster.

A worker running on your machine against a remote model server is still a local worker: inference and tool execution are separate choices. To run the worker process on another machine, use the [fleet configuration](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html).

## Choose capabilities deliberately

Clio Coder supports more than one kind of model interaction. Its Inception runtime serves [Mercury diffusion language models](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/diffusion-models.html) as chat models with tool calling. Optional, experimental [System One routes](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html) answer typed questions an agent asks through `consult`. Neither replaces a chat model or is required to get started.

Vision support depends on the model and the route. A model advertised as multimodal is not enough if the bridge does not carry images: the managed Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Antigravity CLI bridges are text-only. Check what the route accepts before attaching a screenshot.

**Know where information goes**

- Clio runs locally, but a configured cloud model receives the input sent to that provider.
- Local inference keeps inference on the selected server; tools, peers, plugins, and commands can still make network requests.
- Clio Coder is Apache 2.0 software. Inference hardware, provider usage, and subscriptions can still cost money.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [Connection guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Install Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/#start)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html

# Coordinate the coding agents you already use

> Use supported coding peers for bounded assignments, distinguish managed runs from interactive handoffs, and review the results before combining them.

You can use Clio Coder to coordinate the coding agents you already have installed. Give a peer a focused assignment, follow a managed run where the connector supports it, and review its output before accepting the change.

**Version scope**

In v0.6.8 the supported peer family includes Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Antigravity. Their modes and controls differ. Install and authenticate each peer's own CLI before configuring it in Clio Coder.

## Before you start

- Clio Coder with one working model connection. The [first session](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html) covers it.
- A peer's CLI installed and signed in under its own account.
- An assignment whose answer you can check against the repository.

## See which peers Clio Coder can use

```sh
clio-coder interop inspect --json
clio-coder configure --interop
```

The first command reports what Clio can find; the second configures interoperability. In a terminal conversation, `/interop` shows the available connections. The [interoperability guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/interop.html) covers the mode for each peer.

![Terminal interop view listing detected coding agents, with the configuration entry that connecting Claude Code would add.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-interop.webp)

*/interop lists the coding agents Clio Coder detected and the entry that connecting would add.*

![Terminal interop inspect report giving each detected peer its ACP, headless, and pane status and the next step for each.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-interop-inspect.webp)

*interop inspect reports each peer's managed, headless, and pane modes and the next step for each.*

What Clio Coder detected on a machine with three peer CLIs installed but not signed in.

## Choose managed work or an interactive handoff

The three commands answer different needs. Pick by whether you want a recorded run or a place to work with the peer yourself.

| Command | What happens | What Clio Coder records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/delegate <peer> <task>` | A configured ACP peer runs the task | The result and a sealed run record |
| `/run --target <target> <agent> <task>` | A configured headless target runs it | The result and a sealed run record |
| `/peer <peer> <brief>` | A Herdr pane opens for you to work in (start Clio Coder inside Herdr with `--with-panes`) | No run record |

Panes are [experimental](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/panes-and-docks.html). Do not infer that a pane completed a task because it opened. Do not infer that a run record contains every internal reasoning step or mediates every operation inside a peer-owned loop.

## Give one bounded assignment

**Assign to a peer**

> Inspect the parser's handling of empty input. Identify the existing tests and propose a regression test. Do not edit files.

That last sentence is a task instruction, not an enforced boundary. Where the peer supports it, add `--read-only` to `/run` or `/delegate`, then confirm in the run's record that the restriction applied. A connector that cannot enforce a restriction is not equivalent to one that can.

## Keep worker authority separate

A native worker inherits the main session's level inside its own permit and OS sandbox, so at `yolo` a mediated worker runs the yolo way within its dispatch scope. A read-only worker stays at `default`. Managed peer dispatches run at default permissions, even when the main session uses `yolo`, and each external agent runs its own tool loop.

Each peer enforces read-only through its own mechanism. Check the mode you select instead of assuming one contract for all of them.

| Peer | Read-only headless run in v0.6.8 |
| --- | --- |
| Codex | Its read-only sandbox mode |
| Claude Code | Plan mode with read tools |
| Antigravity | Its plan and sandbox route |
| Pi | Read tools |
| OpenCode | Refused before launch |

ACP peers may own their tools. Explicitly permitting peer-owned tools changes what Clio can observe and mediate, so read the guide's permission limits before using such a peer on sensitive work. Clio Coder's own session is not an operating-system sandbox. Native workers run their commands in one when it is available, and external peers keep their own authority.

## Separate changes with a worktree

For supported headless dispatch, `--worktree` keeps a Git task branch for review. That helps you compare two proposed changes without mixing their working files.

A worktree is an organizational boundary. It does not confine a peer's filesystem or network access. Keep assignments narrow, inspect the branch and diff, and run the repository's checks before merging a result.

## Review before combining

**What to look for**

A useful result may be a diagnosis, a patch, or a failed attempt that reveals a missing dependency. Look for the files it touched, the checks it ran, and the limits of its report. A claimed test result and an observed check are different evidence.

When comparing agents, give them the same task and evaluate the actual output. Record the model, connector, setup, check results, and any costs you can substantiate. Clio Coder coordinating two peers does not make either one better.

**Boundaries**

- Supported modes differ by peer, and some cannot receive live steering.
- A pane is an interactive handoff; it produces no run record.
- Peer accounts, subscriptions, and usage limits stay with each peer's own provider.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [Project quality checks](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html)
- [Interoperability guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/interop.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html

# Keep a long coding task on track

> Inspect context, preserve decisions through a handoff, and resume the correct branch without turning every past message into a current instruction.

Long coding work needs more than saved chat history. You need the current objective, the decisions that still apply, the relevant files, and the checks left to run. Clio Coder gives you controls for inspecting that context and continuing after a session grows.

**Version scope**

This guide describes the v0.6.8 context workflow. It does not promise that every detail survives summarization or that a model cannot misunderstand a handoff.

**Four controls for a long task**

1. Inspect (/context): Usage, reserved output, remaining headroom, and any pending handoff.
2. Reduce (/context compact): A focused summary that keeps what you name. Moves from the previous stage: history grows.
3. Hand off (/handoff): A continuation bound to this branch and its decisions. Moves from the previous stage: the work continues.
4. Recover (/context recover): Reduce or deliver, chosen explicitly by its ID. Moves from the previous stage: a transition stops.

*Inspect first; reduce, hand off, or recover only for a stated reason.*

## Give the project a starting point

A project handbook orients the model toward the repository's structure and rules. The context commands prepare a `CLIO-CODER.md` handbook and a structural code index called the codemap.

```sh
clio-coder context init
clio-coder context index
```

Review generated project material as you would any other change. Keep build commands and verification expectations specific to the project: an incorrect handbook makes the wrong answer easier to repeat.

The codemap locates structural information without reading every file into the conversation. It does not replace reading a function before changing its behavior. Legacy codewiki files remain readable; new output uses codemap.

## Inspect before the context fills

In the terminal, `/context` shows usage, output reservation, remaining headroom, and any pending handoff. On the desktop alpha, the Session column has **Context** and **Branches** cards, and typing `/` in the composer offers `/context`, `/tree`, `/fork`, and `/handoff`.

![Terminal Context Window dock showing the usage grid and 12,566 of 808,704 tokens in use, with the system prompt and tool definitions listed.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-context.webp)

*/context: the probed window, tokens in use, and what fills them.*

![Terminal tree view of a forked conversation, noting which session it was forked from and listing the turns.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-tree.webp)

*/tree after /fork: the branch records where it came from, and /resume reaches the turns left behind.*

The terminal's context window, and a forked conversation in /tree.

Watch what you are accumulating. A large test log, an old exploration branch, and a current design decision should not carry the same weight. Ask the agent to cite the file or tool result behind an important conclusion instead of a remembered paraphrase.

## Reduce with a stated purpose

```text
/context compact Keep the objective, decisions, changed files, test results, and remaining work.
```

**After compaction**

Read the continuation. Compaction reduces history; it does not prove that the model kept every fact. If an important constraint disappears, restate it with its source.

## Hand off a defined continuation

`/handoff <goal>` prepares a continuation around a stated goal. A useful goal says what the receiving session should do next and which work must stay intact.

**Example handoff goal**

> /handoff Fix the empty-input parser bug: keep the failing case in tests/parser.test.ts, the chosen approach of validating before tokenizing, and rerun the parser tests before finishing.

Handoffs are bound to the active branch and its decisions. A fork can recall earlier notes without inheriting permission to resume its parent's pending transition. Use `/tree` and `/fork` deliberately, and confirm which branch you are continuing. To return to a session after quitting, type the `/resume <id>` line from the exit summary; a prefix works when it matches one session.

## Recover an interrupted transition explicitly

If `/context` shows a pending handoff, use its exact ID:

```text
/context recover <handoffId> reduce
/context recover <handoffId> deliver
```

These are two different recoveries, not two commands to run in turn. Choose **reduce** when the reduction has not committed and another attempt remains; choose **deliver** when the validated commit exists. The [continuity guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html) explains those states.

A restarted process records an interrupted handoff as paused and waits for your command. Do not create a new handoff just because a pending one looks unfamiliar.

## Keep memory reviewable

Proactive memory is separate from the working context. Open `/memory` and use its **Review** tab to approve a proposed lesson with `a` or reject it with `x`; an observation about one repository should not quietly become a rule for every project.

Global, procedural, runtime, and agent lessons wait for you. A repository knowledge lesson can be approved automatically once a session records that it held with no contradiction, and a later contradiction demotes it.

In `/settings`, **Memory connection** and **Memory model** choose where memory's model calls run. With neither set, memory uses your chat route and spends model calls there. Turning **Proactive memory** off stops those calls, along with task memory and the memory section of the prompt.

Stored memory is not fine-tuning of the underlying model. Its value depends on selection, scope, and whether it is still relevant.

**Boundaries**

- A summary is a model's reduction, so check it against sources when it matters.
- A handoff belongs to the branch that prepared it; a fork recalls its notes but cannot resume it.
- Only approved lessons influence later sessions, and a repository knowledge lesson can be approved automatically, so check `/memory`.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [Continuity guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html)
- [Resource Library](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/resource-library.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html

# Check a change against your repository

> Declare which checks matter, run them through verification, and inspect whether passing results still match the files you are reviewing.

A useful coding result includes more than "done." You need to know what changed, which checks ran, and whether those results still apply to the files you are reviewing. Clio Coder v0.6.8 can use your repository's declared checks and a project quality policy to make those questions explicit.

**What this establishes**

Recorded verification is evidence about named checks and named inputs. It is not proof of correctness; your tests still need to cover the behavior that matters.

## Before you start

- A Git repository with a test or build check it already declares, such as a package script or a CI step.
- Clio Coder with a model that supports tool calling.
- Time to read the resolved command before you approve it.

## Start with checks the project already owns

The verifier derives checks from supported build systems, project scripts, and CI definitions. When it cannot resolve a requested check, it should not substitute an arbitrary command and call it a pass.

**Ask Clio**

> Run this project's test check through verify. Report its exit status, failures, and anything you could not check.

![Terminal turn in which Clio Coder runs the test check through verify with exit 0 and reports zero failures, the seven passing tests, and what it could not check.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-verify-result.webp)

*The test check through verify, and a report of its exit status, failures, and limits.*

The same request in the temperature-calibration example, with the check's working directory named.

Read the resolved command and working directory before approving execution. `verify` is subject to command admission: naming a check does not grant permission to run it, and a denied command is not a validation result.

When a command needs your approval, the terminal card names the tool, the exact command, and, for commands it recognizes, an **Effect** line in plain words.

![Terminal approval card for git push origin main with an Effect line reading Publishes to origin, and the allow, inspect, stop, and deny keys.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-approval-effect.webp)

*A shell approval card names the command and its effect before anything runs.*

The [tools guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html) covers discovery and execution. The [temperature-calibration example](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html) follows a small numerical correction with recorded test results.

## Declare what particular changes require

A quality policy selects required checks by changed path. At the Git workspace root:

```yaml title=.clio-coder/quality.yaml
version: 1
rules:
  - id: source
    paths: ["src/**", "tests/**"]
    inputs: ["src/**", "tests/**", "package.json", "package-lock.json"]
    checks: [test]
    allowLimitations: false
```

### Name the changes a rule covers

`paths` selects the rule: here, any change under `src/` or `tests/`.

### List every input the result depends on

`inputs` feeds freshness. Include fixtures, configuration, helper files, and lockfiles; this example assumes the root package declares a `test` script and uses that lockfile.

### Name existing checks, not commands

`checks` refers to declared checks. A policy cannot insert an arbitrary shell command or bypass approvals.

### Decide whether limitations are acceptable

`allowLimitations: false` means a reported limitation does not satisfy the rule.

Clio Coder does not write this policy for you. Review it as a repository contract: a command that passes a narrow subset of tests should not satisfy a policy that requires the full declared test check.

## Inspect freshness after editing

**When a passing check still counts**

1. Declared check (Your project): A package script, build target, or CI definition the project already owns.
2. Recorded pass (Results): Stored with source, check-declaration, and policy fingerprints. Moves from the previous stage: verify runs it.
3. Stale (Assessment): The earlier pass no longer describes the files. Moves from the previous stage: an input changes.
4. Current (Assessment): A result for the work that exists now. Moves from the previous stage: verify runs again.

*A recorded result belongs to the inputs it ran against; an edit to those inputs makes it stale until the check runs again.*

Clio Coder compares source, check-declaration, and policy fingerprints. A passing check becomes stale after relevant inputs change, and a later failure supersedes an earlier pass of the same check.

This matters during an iterative fix. The agent might run a test, make another edit, and then summarize the earlier success. The current assessment should describe the work that exists now, not the best result observed along the way.

Required checks run through `verify` without argument or working-directory overrides. Declare subproject checks with the correct working directory in the supported catalog or a root script. The [quality-policy guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html) explains check identity and freshness.

## Read the result where you work

On the desktop alpha, the Session column's **Artifacts** card lists outputs and session records, **Changes** lists the files a turn changed, and **Evidence** appears once a run has a record. In the terminal, `/view` opens artifacts and run records.

![Terminal View dock with the transcript list on the left and, on the right, the recorded verify call: check test, its working directory, exit 0, and the passing test lines.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-view-result.webp)

*/view keeps the recorded check, its working directory, and its output.*

**What to look for**

The actual check, its result, and any missing evidence. A sealed run record is an inspectable account of the run, and `clio-coder telemetry verify` checks its journals. It is not a certificate that every scientific or operational requirement was met.

**Boundaries**

- Snapshots need Git and a workspace at the repository root. They cover tracked and nonignored untracked source within the documented bounds.
- They do not establish the state of external datasets, installed dependencies, running services, or other hidden inputs.
- A valid policy selects high rigor by default and asks to continue for outstanding checks when recovery is possible; normal rigor makes the assessment advisory. Neither grants extra execution authority.
- Numerical comparisons, integration tests, and human review may still be necessary.

**Next steps**

- [A numerical change, checked with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html)
- [Quality policy guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/quality-policy.html)
- [Install Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/#start)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/add-skills-and-plugins-deliberately.html

# Add skills and plugins deliberately

> Preview a project-scoped skill or plugin, inspect its package pin, and load the resources your task needs without treating an installation as a permission grant.

Clio Coder's Library contains skills, agents, prompts, playbooks, and plugins. You can add a procedure to one project or install it for your user. Preview what will be written, inspect the resource, and load it when a task needs it.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. Library recipes and extensions have different roles, and installing either is not a grant of authority.

**From the catalog to one task**

1. Browse (/library or Alt+L): Catalog content that ships with Clio Coder; nothing is installed yet.
2. Preview (Install review): Destination, dependencies, scope, and the package pin. Moves from the previous stage: --dry-run.
3. Pinned copy (Project or user scope): Drifted content is blocked from loading. Moves from the previous stage: install.
4. Loaded for a task (One conversation): Recipes load on demand. Moves from the previous stage: /skill.

*Installing a package makes it available; a task loads what it needs. Neither step grants extra authority.*

## Browse what ships with Clio Coder

Open `/library` in the terminal or press Alt+L. On the desktop alpha, the Library page lists the catalog with an **Installed only** filter. In the terminal, **Browse** shows available content and **Installed** manages your copies.

![Terminal Library on the Skills tab filtered to tdd: the bundled skill package, not installed, with its origin and source.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-library-skill-tdd.webp)

*The Library in Browse mode, filtered to the bundled tdd skill package.*

## Preview a small addition

### Preview the install

Start with a resource you can evaluate, such as the shipped test-driven-development skill:

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:tdd --project --dry-run
```

Check the destination, dependencies, scope, and package pin. The `--json` form carries the full plan.

![Terminal running the tdd skill install as a dry run, then the JSON plan showing its project destination, bundled source with sha256, valid content, and no dependencies.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-library-dry-run.webp)

*A dry run plans the project install; the JSON plan shows the destination, source, and package hash.*

### Install it for this project

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:tdd --project
```

The first project install in a workspace is yours, so Clio Coder approves the project's packages for that workspace. After that, a changed project package set, including one that arrives with a clone or a pull, is listed but not loaded until you review it with `clio-coder config trust plugins` and approve the digest it prints.

### Load it for one concrete task

```text
/skill tdd Add coverage for this parser before changing its behavior.
```

![Terminal Library Installed view with the tdd skill at project scope: how to use it, its availability, source, and origin.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-library-installed.webp)

*Installed at project scope: how to use the skill and where it came from.*

**What installing establishes**

The skill is available and pinned. Installing it does not establish that it writes the right tests; review its instructions, the resulting changes, and the recorded checks. The [Library guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/resource-library.html) covers the current controls.

## Choose project or user scope

Project packages take precedence over matching user packages, and a disabled project copy also suppresses the user copy. A project can therefore keep a resource unavailable instead of inheriting it from one developer's setup.

| Scope | Who it serves | What takes precedence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project | Everyone working in this repository | A matching project package, even when disabled |
| User | You, across projects | Used when the project has no matching package |

Scope helps reproducibility: another person can see which procedures belong to the project. It is not a filesystem sandbox, and the project's normal execution and tool controls still apply.

## Use plugins for related resources

A Library plugin groups related skills, prompts, agents, playbooks, and supporting files. The catalog ships with Clio Coder, but its content is not installed automatically.

```sh
clio-coder library list --kind plugin
clio-coder library install plugin:materio --dry-run
```

![Terminal listing the two bundled plugins, materio and wtfp, with versions and descriptions, neither installed.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-library-list-plugin.webp)

*The bundled plugins, listed without installing them.*

Review the bundle before installing it, and add `--project` when it should belong to the workspace. Local bundles use the same review flow; the [plugin guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html) covers structure and lifecycle.

Installation records a pin over the complete package tree, and drifted content is blocked from loading. Verifying a pin is not a way to approve arbitrary edits to an installed package; use the documented update and review workflow.

## Keep discovery separate from loading

A large Library should not mean every resource enters every model request. The coordinator starts with a smaller attached toolkit and discovers secondary capabilities when a task calls for them, and recipes load on demand.

Write clear resource descriptions and narrow procedures. A skill that explains one project's numerical-test conventions is easier to select and inspect than a bundle that promises to solve every task.

After changes made by another process, `/library reload` refreshes recipes and `/skill off` clears an active skill's armed tool surface. Neither erases earlier instructions from the conversation, and disabling a resource does not stop a tool already running.

## Know when you need an extension

Library plugins provide portable recipes. [Extensions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html) are code that adds runtime tools, hooks, or interface behavior through `clio-coder extensions`, and load only after you approve the capabilities they declare.

Adding tool schemas requires a new session; reloading recipes does not change them. Project extensions follow the same trust rule through `clio-coder config trust extensions`, and Clio Coder names any it ignored when a session starts.

**Boundaries**

- Choose the least extensive mechanism that supplies the task.
- Workspace trust decides whether project packages load. It does not review them for you.
- Review executable code before using it, and account for its commands and network access under your own machine's permissions.
- A bigger Library helps only when it serves a better-defined task.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [Library guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/resource-library.html)
- [Plugin guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html

# Work from a laptop with remote workers

> Use a local Clio Coder session to coordinate SSH workers when your machines share the required project path, runtime version, and approved access.

Your conversation can stay on your laptop while a worker runs tools on another machine. Register an SSH node, install the exact Clio Coder build if needed, verify its project and model route, then choose where the first bounded task runs.

**Version scope**

This guide describes the v0.6.8 fleet. Remote workers use your existing SSH access. They do not grant access to institutional systems or replace their scheduler and data rules.

## Before you start

- Noninteractive SSH access to a machine you may use for work.
- Clio Coder on the node at exactly your client's version. To let Clio install it, the node needs Node.js 22.19 or newer and npm on its noninteractive SSH PATH.
- The project at the same absolute path on the client and node, using shared storage or matching clean Git checkouts.
- A model route the worker can reach from the node.

## Choose where each part runs

**One remote task**

1. Session (Your laptop): The conversation, your approvals, and the dispatch.
2. Worker (Fleet node): Runs at default authority in the same absolute project path. Moves from the previous stage: SSH dispatch.
3. Inference (The worker's route): A localhost address resolves on the node, not on your laptop. Moves from the previous stage: model requests.

*The conversation stays on your laptop, the worker runs its tools on the node, and the worker's model route resolves from the node.*

Worker placement and inference are separate. A local worker calling a remote model endpoint runs tools locally. An SSH worker runs tools on the selected node. A target URL containing `localhost` refers to the worker's machine.

Choose a node for the compiler, filesystem, data or capacity the task needs. Declared labels such as `gpu` help describe it, but they do not prove observed hardware or available memory. A remote worker using a cloud target can send model input to that provider under the existing information policy.

## Add one SSH node

From your project root, register an SSH alias, hostname or address:

```sh
clio-coder fleet nodes add build-node --host build-node --max-workers 1
clio-coder fleet nodes list
```

The implicit `local` node already exists. Adding a node keeps unpinned work local. The new node starts as **not checked**.

Use an existing SSH alias to select the user, port and identity. You can also pass `--user`, `--port` and `--identity-file` explicitly. `--labels cpu,build` adds operator declarations. Start with one slot until you know the node's workload and resource limits.

In the terminal, open `/settings fleet` and choose **Add SSH node**. The guided flow asks for a name and host, then offers to test and record readiness or to preview an installation. Open a node row to see evidence and timestamps, test it, preview an install or remove its saved entry. A test started here always records its result.

![Terminal Settings open on Fleet, with the default worker connection and model, thinking level, worker location, the local node, and run limits.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-settings-fleet.webp)

*Settings: worker defaults, nodes, and limits under Fleet.*

### Use a LAN endpoint or optional Tailscale discovery

If the client and node share a network, prefer a LAN endpoint you have verified with SSH. Otherwise, a reachable Tailscale address or MagicDNS name can use the same worker transport.

```sh
clio-coder fleet nodes discover
clio-coder fleet nodes add travel-node --host travel-node.example-tailnet.ts.net
```

Discovery is opt-in. It reads `tailscale status --json` when the CLI is installed and signed in, lists MagicDNS names and IP addresses, and leaves the selection to you. The TUI's **Discover with Tailscale** lets you pick an endpoint and name the node. A discovered peer has no proven SSH access, runtime or project readiness. You can add an SSH host directly without Tailscale.

The endpoint can matter substantially. In one measurement on this project's development network, a 4 MiB SSH transfer ran at about **173 MiB/s over LAN and 1.4 MiB/s over Tailscale**. SSH setup and existing connection multiplexing affect those numbers; measure your own route. Clio Coder uses the host you configure and does not automatically switch between addresses.

## Install the exact client build

If the node lacks a matching Clio Coder runtime, preview a user-level install:

```sh
clio-coder fleet nodes install build-node
```

Review the package size, digest and destination. Then execute it:

```sh
clio-coder fleet nodes install build-node --yes
```

Clio Coder packs the build the client actually runs, transfers it over SSH, checks its SHA-256 digest, and installs it under the node's `~/.local/share/clio-coder/workers/<digest>/`. The install uses the node's existing Node.js and npm, verifies the version and updates the saved worker entry. The installer does not require sudo or modify services or shell profiles. Optional SDK dependencies are omitted.

You can also manage Clio Coder yourself, for example with the standard installer on a cluster login node, whose private Node.js is not on `PATH`. The default invocation is `clio-coder worker`. A custom `--entry` needs an explicit `--version-command` that reports its Clio Coder version; it cannot skip version verification.

## Prepare and verify the project

Choose one supported arrangement:

| Arrangement | What Clio Coder verifies | Available work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared storage at the same absolute path | A transient client-side file challenge is visible from the node. | Read-only and mutating workers use that storage. |
| Independent checkout at the same absolute path | Both trees are clean, have the same Git HEAD and matching root history. | Read-only work; mutations through an isolated task worktree and SSH commit return. |

Clio does not clone an arbitrary repository, map different paths, install project dependencies or stage datasets. Prepare those yourself. For independent checkouts, update both to the same clean baseline before testing.

### Observe first

```sh
clio-coder fleet nodes test build-node
clio-coder doctor
```

These commands observe the node without creating directories there or granting new dispatch eligibility. A plain test can identify a clean matching checkout; recording also permits the transient client-side challenge that proves shared storage.

Model facts distinguish network reachability, access to the model listing, model presence and runtime support. Unknown remains unknown; a catalog listing is not a successful generation or proof of a resident model.

![Terminal doctor report with OK rows for the version, the installer install with its private Node.js runtime, directories, credentials, migrations, sessions, and local worker capacity.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-doctor.webp)

*doctor on an installer install: version, install method and runtime, directories, and local worker capacity.*

### Record readiness for this project

```sh
clio-coder fleet nodes test build-node --record
clio-coder fleet nodes list
```

A passing recorded check makes the node **ready for this project**. A failed recorded check revokes previous eligibility. Records expire after one day and bind the entire connection configuration and client version. Changing the host, user, port, key or worker entry requires another recorded check.

`doctor --fix` can record all node checks, along with its broader local repairs. Run plain `doctor` first to review those repairs. The node-specific test is the focused route when you only want to record one node.

### Refresh after an upgrade or endpoint change

Install the new exact client build when needed, then repeat the recorded test from the project root. A pinned task with an invalid or expired check fails with a reason; it does not silently run elsewhere.

## Choose the first worker

Keep the first task read-only and familiar. For example, ask Clio Coder:

```text
Use a read-only Scout to inspect the README and explain this project's test command.
Before dispatching, ask me once where to run it, offering local and suitable verified fleet nodes.
```

When a verified node suits substantial work and no preference or pin exists, Clio asks once for the session. The choice remembers the exact node id for later unpinned work. The question does not replace the existing dispatch-plan approval. If you explicitly request `build-node`, Clio can pin it directly.

A **Standing worker node preference** in Fleet settings persists across sessions. Placement priority is an explicit task node, a profile pin, the session choice, the standing preference, then local. Headless runs never ask; configure a preference or explicit pin before running them.

Remote workers run under their own permits. The safety judge does not answer for a remote placement, so at `default` a remote worker's ordinary ask is denied. Worker slots limit concurrency; they do not create a scheduler allocation. On a university or laboratory cluster, use an approved execution environment. The [Slurm guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html) describes separate allocation-aware tooling.

## Return edits from an independent checkout

An editing dispatch to an independent node checkout must use `worktree: true`. Ask Clio Coder to use an isolated task worktree, name the files the worker may change and declare the host checks you want before application.

Clio creates a matching branch and worktree on the node at the approved baseline. After the worker exits, Clio commits its edits there, fetches the branch through the existing SSH connection and checks the returned baseline and permitted paths.

The commit is imported into the owned local task worktree before the existing host verification and guarded apply flow. `apply: "preserve"` keeps the result without merging it.

Transfer, verification and application failures preserve the node branch for recovery. The run record names the node, branch, worktree and returned commit when available. Inspect preserved work before merging or deleting it. A successful guarded merge permits remote cleanup. The node's original checkout stays at its old baseline, so update it deliberately before the next dispatch that needs the new commit.

## Follow the result

Open **Workers** with Alt+W to see queued, active, failed and completed work with its actual node. Inside Herdr with panes on, the same key opens a [live dashboard](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/panes-and-docks.html) beside the conversation. Review the worker result, receipt and project changes. The CLI's `clio-coder fleet status` and `clio-coder fleet view <runId>` expose durable results from another terminal.

SSH nodes and delegated peers are separate execution paths. A delegated peer is not an SSH machine whose resources or project access Clio Coder has verified.

## On a cluster

```sh
curl -fsSL https://coder.iowarp.ai/install.sh | sh
```

The installer needs no root, refuses to run under sudo, and brings a private Node.js 24. On x64 login nodes with glibc from 2.17 to 2.27 it selects a compatible Node.js build. Behind a proxy, export `https_proxy` first; the cluster guide lists the variables for mirrored and offline installs.

That private Node.js is not added to `PATH`. A node installed this way already has Clio Coder, so skip `fleet nodes install` there and keep its version equal to your client's.

Clio Coder does not submit jobs for its own workers. Scheduler work goes through the clio-kit Slurm tools, which the agent calls to submit, list, describe, and cancel jobs, each with your approval.

**Boundaries**

- SSH access, exact Clio Coder version and the same absolute project path remain prerequisites.
- Project dependencies and datasets need your own staging; there is no arbitrary repository sync or path mapping.
- Independent-checkout edits require isolated task worktrees and the existing verification and application gates.
- Institutional access rules and schedulers still govern where work may run.
- Worker slots limit concurrency. They are not an allocation, and a login node is not a compute node.
- A remote worker sandboxes its commands only when bubblewrap is present on that node.
- A worker that uses a cloud model sends its input to that provider from the node.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [Fleet guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Install on a cluster](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)
- [Slurm workflows](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html)
- [Install Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/#start)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html

# Write an extension with declared capabilities

> Scaffold, test, and install a small extension, and see exactly what approving its capabilities covers.

A plugin carries content such as skills and prompts. An extension is code: it runs in its own process, declares everything it may do, and loads only after you approve those capabilities. This guide scaffolds a small extension, tests it, installs it, and shows what the approval covers.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8, runtime api 2. The runtime runs inside bubblewrap on Linux or Seatbelt on macOS when a backend exists. Check `/extensions` for the confinement your host gives it.

## Before you start

- Clio Coder installed, on Linux or macOS for a confined runtime.
- Node.js and a little TypeScript. The scaffold includes an entrypoint and a test.

### Scaffold a package

```sh
clio-coder extensions init lint-status --template status
```

This creates the package under `.clio-coder/dev/extensions/lint-status/` and prints the next commands; `--dir` puts it elsewhere. The templates are `status`, `hook`, `panel`, `tool`, and `workspace`. Each gives you a manifest, a TypeScript entrypoint, and a test.

### Read the manifest

`clio-coder-extension.yaml` holds the declaration. Clio Coder discovers and validates it without importing or executing package code. The `runtime` block is the capability envelope, which is the part you consent to.

### Validate and test

```sh
clio-coder extensions validate .clio-coder/dev/extensions/lint-status
clio-coder extensions test .clio-coder/dev/extensions/lint-status
```

Tests can use the package's test host, which drives the same registration code the runtime uses, with in-memory state and a fake clock.

### Install and review

```sh
clio-coder extensions install .clio-coder/dev/extensions/lint-status
```

The install prints what the package would be allowed to do, then records the digest of that envelope. If the manifest changes between review and apply, the install refuses and asks for a fresh review.

### Use and manage it

```text
/extensions
/extensions reload
```

`/extensions` shows each package's state, generation, failures, commands, and confinement. From the shell, use `clio-coder extensions list`, `disable`, `enable`, and `remove`.

![Terminal output: extensions init creates lint-status, validate prints its capability envelope with exec and net false, its SHA-256, and a passed registration check, and test reports one test passed.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-extension-validate.webp)

*Validate prints the capability envelope you are consenting to, before anything is installed.*

**What you should see**

The extension listed with its confinement, and its status in the session. This shows it loaded under the approved envelope. It does not make the code safe, so review what you install as you would any dependency.

## Choose plugin or extension

| You want to | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Share skills, prompts, agents, or playbooks | A plugin |
| Add a hook on a tool call, a runtime tool, a panel, or a timer | An extension |
| Add both, under one name | A plugin paired with an extension |

A project's own extensions also need `clio-coder config trust extensions`. To try ideas without installing, a folder under `.clio-coder/dev/extensions/<id>/` is a dev extension for the terminal session, in a workspace whose project extensions you trust.

**Boundaries**

- Without a sandbox backend, an extension runtime runs with your permissions.
- Dev extensions load in terminal sessions. The desktop Library shows the terminal command for extension lifecycle actions.
- Reinstalling changed content needs a fresh approval.

**Next steps**

- [Add skills and plugins deliberately](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/add-skills-and-plugins-deliberately.html)
- [Install plugins](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/plugins.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/diffusion-models.html

# Diffusion models in the terminal

> Connect Inception's Mercury models for chat and workers, and watch an answer refine as a whole instead of arriving token by token.

Most language models write an answer one token at a time. A diffusion language model starts from a rough version of the whole answer and refines it in a few passes. Clio Coder can use Inception's Mercury models this way, for chat and for workers, with tool calling.

**Version scope**

The `inception` runtime has shipped since v0.5.3 and this article describes v0.6.8. The frame-by-frame display exists only in the terminal, and diffusion models are less tested on long agentic work than the models most people use.

## Before you start

- An Inception account and API key, exported as `INCEPTION_API_KEY`.
- Permission to send this project's code to that provider.
- Clio Coder in the terminal, if you want to watch the answer refine.

## Connect Mercury

Run guided setup, choose **A provider account or API**, then Inception:

```sh
clio-coder configure
```

Or add the target directly:

```sh
clio-coder targets add --id mercury --runtime inception --model mercury-3 --api-key-env INCEPTION_API_KEY
```

The runtime lists `mercury-3`, its default, `mercury-2.5`, `mercury-2`, and `mercury-edit-2`. Setup reads each model's context window and output limit from the provider's model list, and fails if the model you named is not on it.

## What you see

In the terminal, each update from the model carries the whole answer so far. Clio Coder replaces the visible text on every frame instead of appending to it, and dims the part that is still changing. There is no progress gauge, because the provider reports none until the last frame.

Tool calls, permission cards, `/view`, and run records work as they do with any chat model. Headless runs, workers, the desktop app, and editors connected over ACP receive an ordinary stream of text.

## Where it fits

A quick whole-answer model suits short, bounded requests: a commit message, an explanation of one function, a first draft to compare. `/draft` uses the active chat model, so with Mercury active it returns several candidates quickly. You can also keep another model for conversation and route selected workers to the Mercury target.

Try it on a task you can check before trusting it with a long one. This page makes no speed or quality claim; measure both on your own repository.

**Boundaries**

- Mercury runs without a thinking level. Clio Coder pins the provider's fastest reasoning setting, because the default spends the output budget on hidden reasoning and can return an empty answer.
- A provider content-filter refusal is shown as a refusal and does not count as a failed connection.
- Inception is a cloud provider. Input you send leaves your machine, and usage is billed by Inception.

**Next steps**

- [Choose a model for your project](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [Connection guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Bring a fast decision model with System One](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html)
