Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/panes-and-docks.html

# Panes and docks: files, workers, and music

> Inside Herdr, show and hide a file browser, a live worker dashboard, and a focus radio beside the conversation with one key each.

When Clio Coder runs inside Herdr, a terminal multiplexer, it can open panes of its own beside the conversation: a file browser below, a live view of workers on the right, and a small radio. Each is a dock. One key shows or hides it, and hiding keeps it running.

**Experimental in v0.6.8**

Panes need the Herdr pane host. On Linux and macOS the first bare `clio-coder` asks once whether to open a workspace, and `interface.panes.enabled: off` stops asking. Music is off until you enable it. Keys, commands, and settings may change. Herdr has no Windows build.

## Before you start

- Herdr, installed with `clio-coder tools install herdr`, and a Herdr session to start Clio Coder in.
- Yazi for the files dock: `clio-coder tools install yazi`.
- cliamp for music: `clio-coder tools install cliamp`.

## Turn panes on

Start one session with panes, from a terminal inside Herdr:

```sh
clio-coder --with-panes
```

To keep them on, set `interface.panes.enabled: auto` and restart. `--no-panes` turns them off for one session. Outside Herdr, including in tmux, there are no docks: `/files` becomes a one-time full-screen picker and Alt+W opens the worker list inside Clio Coder.

## Three docks, one habit

| Dock | Key | Where it opens | Also enable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workers | Alt+W | Right of the conversation | Nothing |
| Files | Alt+E | Below | `interface.panes.files.enabled` |
| Music | Alt+A | A thin strip below | `integrations.music.enabled` |

Press the key once to show a dock and again to hide it. A hidden dock moves to a parked tab and keeps its state: the file browser stays in its directory and the radio keeps playing. Press the key twice quickly to close the dock and end its program. Quitting Clio Coder closes all of them.

Drag a divider to resize a dock; the size is kept when you hide and show it. A dock never takes more than half the window, and one that cannot fit says how much room it needs. `/panes` prints which docks are visible, hidden, or closed. The same keys are under Ctrl+G, then `w`, `e`, or `a`.

## Pick files with Yazi

`/files` or Alt+E opens Yazi and moves the keyboard into it. Select files and press Ctrl+Y. Clio Coder appends them to your draft as `@path` references and returns you to the composer without sending anything. One pick carries up to 32 paths.

Yazi runs on a profile and theme that Clio Coder generates, so your own Yazi configuration is untouched. Set `interface.panes.files.profile: user` to use yours instead. `/files hide` and `/files close` do what the key does.

## Watch workers live

Alt+W opens a dashboard with one card per worker in this session: the agent and task, its state, the model, tool calls against its budget, tokens, cost when it is known, and what the worker is doing now. Running workers come first.

Move with the arrow keys and press Enter to fill the dock with one worker's live stream; Escape returns to the cards. `q` hides the dock. The dashboard only reads recorded run files, so it cannot change a run, and it does not open by itself when a worker starts.

## Play focus radio

`/music` or Alt+A opens cliamp in a strip tall enough for its spectrum bars and starts a lo-fi stream.

```text
/music pause
/music next
/music station Groove Salad
/music off
```

`next` steps through six built-in focus stations. `station` takes a stream URL or a station name; a name that is not built in is looked up in the public Radio Browser directory. Clio Coder keeps its player configuration separate from your own cliamp setup.

The model cannot touch the player unless you also set `integrations.music.agentControl: true` and restart. Then a `music` tool can play, pause, skip, and stop, but not choose stations. When to use it is up to your project instructions.

**Boundaries**

- Docks need Herdr with a recent protocol; an older Herdr can open panes but cannot hide them.
- Station lookup by name and the streams themselves use the network.
- `/peer` opens another coding agent in a pane for you to work in. It is a handoff with no run record.

**Next steps**

- [Files and terminal panes guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html)
- [Coordinate the coding agents you already use](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html)
- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html

# Keep named files with the models you chose

> Declare which paths and tool results may reach which model targets, approve the policy, and see a request to any other destination refused.

Some files should reach only a model you chose. An information-flow rule names a source, such as everything under `secrets/`, and the destinations its content may go to. Once a session has read that source, Clio Coder refuses to send the conversation anywhere else, in every permission mode.

**Advanced, described for v0.6.8**

Information flow does nothing until a project declares source rules and you approve them. The policy format is new and may change. It tracks what a session has read; it is not an operating-system sandbox.

## Before you start

- A project where specific paths or tool results must stay with specific models.
- A configured target for each allowed model, usually a local or institutional one.
- A restart after you approve the policy.

## Declare a source and where it may go

This policy keeps anything read under `secrets/` on one local model target:

```yaml title=.clio-coder/safety.yaml
version: 1
informationFlow:
  targets:
    local:
      runtime: llamacpp
      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1
  recipients:
    private-models: ["target:local"]
  sources:
    - id: secrets-local
      paths: [secrets/]
      recipients: ["group:private-models"]
```

A target is pinned by runtime and endpoint, so pointing the same name at another URL does not keep the approval. A source can also be a tool or an MCP server, and `recipients: []` means the content may go nowhere.

## Review and approve

### Show what would be approved

```sh
clio-coder config trust safety
```

This prints the policy files, their digest, and the exact approval command. It changes nothing.

### Approve those exact bytes

```sh
clio-coder config trust safety --hash <reviewed-sha256>
```

Approval belongs to this workspace and this content. Restart Clio Coder to load it.

An edit you have not approved can only restrict more: a new, unapproved rule labels content and allows no destination.

## What happens in a session

Reading `secrets/notes.txt` labels the session with `secrets-local`. Requests to the pinned `local` target continue. Switch to a cloud model and the next request is refused before it is sent, with the rule, the source, and the allowed destinations named.

The label follows the session through summaries, compaction, resume, branches, and worker results. Changing the model, the policy, or the permission mode does not clear it. To work without it, start a new session.

**Workers and other agents**

Native workers check each model request. Coding agents that make their own model calls, such as Claude Code or Codex, are refused at launch when any rule does not allow their target, and ACP agents and pane peers are refused.

**Boundaries**

- Labels apply to the whole session, not to individual passages.
- Shell commands are observed conservatively and incompletely. A read hidden in a script, a variable, or a `cd` is not reliably seen.
- A rule controls where content may go. Whether a file may be read at all is still decided by permissions.

**Next steps**

- [Tools and permissions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Information flow guide in the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/2c17ee86e5119ddba8aa0e5be109ec7c74b85ab7/docs/guide/information-flow.md)
- [Choose a model for your project](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/semantic-context-and-recordings.html

# Search your project by meaning and record worker runs

> Index code, memory, evidence, and registered experiment folders with a local embedding model, and attach a redacted terminal recording to a dispatched worker's evidence.

Clio Coder 0.6.2 can keep a local index of your project that you search by meaning instead of exact words. It covers code maps, wiki pages, approved memory, evidence bundles, recorded worker output, and folders of experiment data you register. Clio Coder can also record what a dispatched worker displayed, as a redacted terminal cast in that run's evidence. Both start off.

**Beta in v0.6.2**

Semantic context and worker recording are new in v0.6.2 and off by default. Commands, supported formats, and the index layout may change between releases. Ordinary startup scans and embeds nothing until you configure the feature.

## Before you start

- A Clio Coder target that serves the EmbeddingGemma 2 Q8 model through a llama.cpp embedding server or a LiteLLM proxy you already run. Clio Coder does not start one.
- The SHA-256 of the model file, and of its multimodal projector if you want images or audio.
- `ffmpeg` on `PATH` if you want still frames sampled from GIF or video files.

## Build an index

### Pin the model and check the route

```sh
clio-coder semantic configure \
  --target local-embed --model embeddinggemma-2-q8 \
  --asset-identity sha256:<model-sha256> \
  --projector-identity sha256:<projector-sha256> \
  --modality text --modality image --modality audio \
  --qualify
```

Use your own target and model names. `--qualify` sends fixed canary requests for each modality you chose and pins the text canary in the profile. It proves that the route accepts those requests and returns vectors of the expected shape. It does not measure retrieval quality, and it cannot read the model file's actual hash.

### Register a folder

```sh
clio-coder semantic inbox preview ./experiment-data
clio-coder semantic inbox add ./experiment-data --id experiments
```

Preview lists file types and the estimated work before anything is saved. Clio Coder honors ignore files, refuses symlinks and credential-shaped files, and applies the project's read policy. It never indexes a folder you did not register. Add `--scope user` to register an inbox for every project.

### Refresh and search

```sh
clio-coder semantic refresh
clio-coder semantic status
clio-coder semantic search "Which run produced the delayed oscillation?" --limit 5
```

`refresh` is an explicit, bounded job. An interrupted or partly failed refresh keeps the last complete generation and reports what is still pending. An unchanged refresh reuses its vectors.

## Read a result

Each hit names the exact path and, where it applies, the line, page, notebook cell, video frame, or audio offset. It carries a short excerpt and the generation it came from, and evidence and recording hits carry an evidence id. Search narrows where to look. Clio Coder still reads the original file, code, or receipt before it makes a claim.

In a session, the agent searches through its `context` tool with bounded filters for source kind, run, dates, media type, and count. A question that mixes a run manifest, a code symbol, and a plot works better as one search per source. If the embedding route is down, search falls back to lexical candidates from the last complete generation.

| Source | Indexed in this beta |
| --- | --- |
| Code and text | Source files, typed code map records, and wiki pages |
| Documents | PDF pages with extractable text, notebook sources and outputs |
| Images | PNG, JPEG, and WebP |
| Audio | Bounded mono 16 kHz WAV |
| Video | Timestamped still frames sampled from GIF, MP4, WebM, and MOV |
| Not supported | Raw video, reasoning across frames, scanned PDF OCR, and other audio formats |

## Keep the index current

Add `--background` to `semantic configure` to refresh at session start and after code map changes. It is off by default, yields to foreground inference, and checkpoints when interrupted. On a shared route that holds one model at a time, weigh the chat load before you turn it on.

The index lives in your cache directory, with one namespace per project and embedding profile. Code, memory, and evidence stay where they are, so deleting the cache removes only derived data.

A changed serving build, model file, projector, or preprocessing recipe needs a new qualification and gets its own namespace. `clio-coder semantic reembed --profile embeddinggemma-2-q8-768 --from <old-profile-identity>` embeds the old records again under the new profile. Old vectors are never copied into it.

## Record a worker run

```sh
clio-coder run --agent scout --record "Check the experiment on the worker node"
```

In a session, the dispatch tool accepts `record: true` for a call or a single task, including work placed on an SSH node. Clio Coder writes a bounded display stream beside the worker's own protocol. It copies a redacted `.cast` into the run's evidence bundle with the run, node, timestamps, byte count, and SHA-256.

A capture error or a partial run is labeled incomplete. The sealed run record, not the recording, decides whether the worker succeeded.

Capture needs no extra program. For playback, `clio-coder tools install asciinema` installs a checksum-pinned asciinema. `clio-coder fleet nodes tools install <node> asciinema` previews the same user-level install on a worker node, and `--yes` performs it without sudo. asciinema is GPL-3.0-or-later, and its license and exact source ship with the pinned install.

**Boundaries**

- Similarity finds candidates. It is not proof of a scientific result or of a worker's success, and run records and memory approval rules stay authoritative.
- Matching model and projector hashes do not make vectors compatible across serving stacks. Keep each stack's index separate.
- An extension can request embeddings only when its manifest declares the service and you approve it, and it never receives the target's credentials.
- A recording is bounded, timed terminal output. It is not a video of the screen.

**Next steps**

- [Semantic context beta guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/v0.6.2/docs/guide/semantic-context.md)
- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)
- [Connect a model](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-on-a-local-model.html

# Run Clio Coder on a local model

> Connect a local server with no account or key, check what Clio Coder learned about it, and see what else to check if code must stay on your machine.

You can run Clio Coder with a model on your own machine, with no account and no API key. This guide connects a local server, checks what Clio Coder learned about it, and shows what else to look at if your code must not leave the machine.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. Supported local servers include Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and Lemonade. Whether a given model handles long agentic work is yours to test, and setup does not test it for you.

## Before you start

- A local server running, with a model that supports tool calling loaded.
- Clio Coder installed, and a repository you know.

## Connect it

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
clio-coder configure
```

Choose **Guided setup**, then **An app on this computer**, or **A model server** for a server elsewhere. Choose **Connect by endpoint** when you already know the URL. LM Studio commonly serves at `http://localhost:1234`, and Ollama at `http://localhost:11434`.

Then select a model that supports tool calling. Setup checks that the server is reachable and reads its catalog. It does not send a generation request or test tool calling, so the first real test comes next.

## Check what Clio Coder learned

```sh
clio-coder targets --json
clio-coder doctor
```

In `targets --json`, `contextWindowProvenance` says where the window figure came from, such as a value the server reported or one you configured. A local server has no fallback number. If a figure looks wrong, set `targets[].capabilities.contextWindow`, or `ollama.numCtx` for Ollama, which is sent with every request.

## Ask something you can check

**Example**

> Read the build configuration and name the command that runs the tests. Run it and report the result. Do not edit files.

**What you should see**

Tool calls that really run, followed by an answer that matches your project. If the model writes out a command as text and never calls a tool, this model or server is not handling tool calls correctly, so try another before going further.

![Terminal transcript in which Qwopus3.8 runs ls, reads package.json, and runs npm test with exit 0, then names npm test as the test command and reports one test passed and none failed.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/tui-local-model-tools.webp)

*Tool calls that really ran on a self-hosted model reached through a LiteLLM gateway, then an answer that matches the project.*

## Keep the work on your machine

A local chat route does not by itself make the whole session local.

- Memory uses the chat route when no memory route is set, so it stays local unless you name another. Compaction does the same unless `context.compaction.model` names another.
- System One is off by default. A hosted route would send data out.
- Web tools, MCP servers, plugins, peers, and shell commands can still make network requests.

To enforce a boundary for named files, use [information-flow rules](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html).

**Boundaries**

- Local inference costs no provider fee, though hardware and power still cost money. `clio-coder usage report` shows these calls as free.
- Local servers vary in how they handle tool calls, cache, and long context. Expect to try more than one model.
- Automatic discovery at startup checks default ports only and takes the first model listed. Set a route with `clio-coder configure` to choose one.

**Next steps**

- [Choose a model for your project](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [Connection guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [When do several agents or small models pay off?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/fleets-and-local-models.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/submit-a-slurm-job.html

# Submit a Slurm job through Clio Coder

> Declare the clio-kit Slurm server, install the skill, and let the agent submit and follow a job, with your approval before it reaches the scheduler.

Clio Coder can submit and follow a Slurm job for you through the clio-kit MCP server, and it asks you before each submission or cancellation. Use this when a task needs real compute and you want the job's outcome reported back into the session.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8. Clio Coder has no scheduler tier of its own: the agent calls the server's tools, and Slurm does the rest. Fleet workers do not submit through Slurm.

## Before you start

- A host where `sbatch`, `squeue`, `scontrol`, and `scancel` reach your cluster.
- An interactive session, since a headless run denies submissions.
- A job script you are willing to run under your allocation.

## Install the server

```sh
uv tool install clio-kit
clio-kit mcp-server slurm
```

The second command lets clio-kit prepare its private runtime, which can take longer than the 15-second bound on a first launch. Stop it with Ctrl-C once it is running.

## Declare it

Run `clio-coder paths` to find your config directory, then add this as `mcp.yaml` there:

```yaml title=mcp.yaml
version: 1
servers:
  - id: slurm
    command: clio-kit
    args: [mcp-server, slurm]
    timeoutMs: 120000
```

Keep the id `slurm`. The skill expects it, and it is what switches on the confirmation for allocations.

```sh
clio-coder doctor --verbose
clio-coder mcp list
```

`doctor --verbose` shows `slurm clio-kit`, `slurm mcp server`, and `slurm scheduler` rows. Those rows are informational or warnings, and they never fail the check.

## Install the skill

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:slurm-jobs --project --dry-run
clio-coder library install skill:slurm-jobs --project
```

![Terminal output: doctor --verbose reports clio-kit and the slurm MCP server as OK and the scheduler as INFO because sbatch and squeue are not on PATH; mcp list shows five slurm tools; the skill install dry run plans skill:slurm-jobs.](https://coder.iowarp.ai/assets/guides/cli-slurm-doctor.webp)

*The setup checks on a machine with no Slurm client: the server is declared, its tools are listed, and doctor says the scheduler is missing.*

## Submit one job

**Example**

> /skill slurm-jobs Run scripts/smoke.sbatch on the debug partition with 2 cores for 5 minutes. Report the exit code and the last lines of stdout.

The skill checks that the server is declared, looks at the partition, and submits once. A permission card appears before the job reaches the scheduler, so read the script, cores, memory, and time limit before you press Enter. It then polls with a growing wait until the job reaches a terminal state, and fetches bounded output.

**What you should see**

The answer ends with a line in this form: `Slurm job <id>: <state>, exit <code>, stdout <path>, stderr <path>`. Check that job id against `squeue` or `sacct` if the result matters.

## Cancel a job

Ask the agent to cancel the job by id. Cancelling also asks first, and the server refuses unless the job id is repeated exactly.

**Boundaries**

- In a headless `clio-coder run`, the ask is denied, so a submission or cancellation never runs there.
- A trust setting cannot make a submission run unasked. The confirmation is attached to the tool name.
- Your site's allocation rules and data policies still apply. A login node is not a compute node.
- This repository ships no copy of the server's schema, so the installed clio-kit version is the authority on tool parameters.

**Next steps**

- [Slurm workflows](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html)
- [Install on a cluster](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)
- [What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/pre-register-a-benchmark.html

# Pre-register a benchmark before you measure

> Use the experiment-protocol skill to lock thresholds, tolerances, and verdict conditions into a contract you commit before any result exists.

A benchmark is easy to fool once you have seen the result. The `experiment-protocol` skill has Clio Coder write down the outcome, thresholds, tolerances, and verdict conditions before any measurement, and then keep to them. Use it for a performance study, a numerical comparison, a parameter sweep, or a solver comparison.

**Version scope**

This guide describes v0.6.8 and skill version 0.3.2. To find out why one output is wrong, use `scientific-debugging` instead, since that is a diagnosis and not an experiment.

## Before you start

- A repository with the code to measure and input data you can checksum.
- A chat route, in the terminal or a headless run.
- An environment you can pin: compiler, flags, package versions, and node class.

## Install the skill

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:experiment-protocol --project --dry-run
clio-coder library install skill:experiment-protocol --project
```

Read the dry run first. It shows the destination and the pin.

## Ask for a pre-registration

**Example**

> /skill experiment-protocol Compare the new solver against the current one on data/mesh-256.h5 for step time and accuracy. Stop after you write the contract so I can review it.

The contract goes in `.clio-coder/validation.yaml`, or `VALIDATION.md` at the repository root. Creating that file raises the session's rigor immediately: from the next turn, completion claims must carry validation evidence or state a limitation.

## Review the contract

This is the step that matters, and it is yours. Check that the contract has each of these:

- **Outcome**: one sentence, with a number.
- **Thresholds**: a minimum below which the result is refuted, a target, and a stretch.
- **Tolerances**: absolute or relative, stated per metric. A bare `1e-6` is not a tolerance.
- **Environment pin**: compiler and flags, versions, node class, and scheduler context.
- **Input identity**: paths with checksums.
- **Verdict conditions**: what makes the result confirmed, refuted, or inconclusive.

Commit it before measuring anything, so the history shows it came first. In a headless run nobody can answer questions, so the skill records unstated details as explicit assumptions. Read those assumptions closely.

## Run it

The skill captures a baseline under the pinned environment, then changes one independent variable per run, and records job ids and node lists where a scheduler is involved. It compares results against the registered thresholds only.

**What you should see**

A verdict of confirmed, refuted, or inconclusive against the numbers you committed, with any deviation logged next to the result. Rejected approaches go in a dead-ends ledger. A refuted result plus a ledger entry is a successful experiment.

**Boundaries**

- Watch for a threshold or tolerance edited after results appeared. The skill treats that as a red flag, and `git log` on the contract shows it.
- A single run on a shared machine does not establish a claim. Size repetitions to the noise.
- Findings outside the registered outcome are exploratory and need their own pre-registration.
- The skill checks process. Whether the tolerance is scientifically right is a judgment for someone who knows the field.

**Next steps**

- [A numerical change, checked with Clio Coder](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html

# Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?

> System One's open questions: evaluating on trajectories, forming better questions, and bringing or one day training a model, with what is measured so far and a first experiment.

Can a small, fast decision model make a coding agent's work better? System One is where Clio Coder asks that question. You bring a model that answers typed questions, and Clio Coder gives the agent a `consult` tool, a screen beside the safety judge, and optional triage of queued messages.

The plumbing has shipped. Whether it helps is still open, and the evidence so far is thin.

**Open question, described for v0.6.8**

System One is off until you name a route, and its keys and tool may change between releases. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome to work on it. All samples below are small, and every experiment on this page is proposed and not yet run.

## The question

Three questions sit inside the big one, and each could come back negative.

- **Trajectories.** With a decision model bound, does the agent take a better path through a task: fewer wrong turns, fewer rounds, and the same or better accepted result?
- **Question formation.** Which questions can a small model answer usefully, and what must the question carry for that to happen?
- **Training.** Could a model trained on agent work outperform a general one on these questions?

## What is measured so far

These were measured on the current design, on small samples. They show what the parts do. None of them shows that System One improves an agent's work.

| Measurement | Result | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filter recall on a file digest, on Jev | 0.77, 0.82, 0.92 | Three sets of 6 queries |
| Filter recall on the first 512 characters, on Jev | 0.65, 0.35, 0.92 | The same three sets |
| Filter recall by query type | 0.92 for what a file is for; at best 0.58 for how it behaves | The same sets |
| Judge screen, on a real Haiku judge | Parked 8 of 8 injected pages | 8 pages |
| Judge screen latency | Screen 104 to 157 ms; judge verdict 938 to 1370 ms | The same run |
| Steering triage, how a message relates to the work | 105 of 105 | The relation pick only |
| `consult` calls with Jev bound | 0 calls | 12 real Haiku sessions, 6 with Jev bound |

Read those together. A digest holds up better than a file's opening characters on two of the three sets and ties on the third. It finds what a file is for and misses much of what a file does, which fits a digest that never carries the body.

Precision is weak. Between a third and more than half of filter matches can be wrong, so a filter can narrow a list and cannot settle anything.

### Filter across routes

These also ran on the current design. They are small samples, and the query sets were regression sets, so they were not independent of the work being tested.

| Route | Recall | Precision | Median latency | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Haiku, as a chat route | 0.81 | 0.68 | 2.5 s | Labels |
| Jev | 0.85 | 0.47 | 163 ms | Probabilities |
| A self-hosted chat model | 0.87 | 0.67 | 6.3 s | Labels |

On 3 fresh queries, with about 3 samples, Haiku scored recall 0.83 and precision 1.00, and Jev scored recall 0.50 and precision 0.26. Those figures moved a long way from the table above, which shows how unstable these numbers are. Do not rank the routes from them.

Jev and other engines whose profile declares real probabilities return a score. Any chat route returns one label per question, so its match has no score, and it never drives the judge screen.

### What the screen result covers

The screen result covers injected pages only, and it says nothing about how often the screen would park an honest page.

The most important number is the last row. Given the tool, the agent did not call it once. Nothing has measured a benefit from `consult`, because none of the measured sessions used it on its own.

### One earlier run, on a design that no longer exists

An on/off evaluation ran the older fixed-site design, where Clio Coder asked its own questions at fixed points in a turn. That design is gone, and so is the run's raw data. Only these numbers remain, so nobody can reanalyze them.

The run used build `jev-1.14.0` with Haiku as the main model, over 24 episodes per arm. Total time with System One on was 1.237 times total time with it off, meaning slower, with an interval of 1.037 to 1.484. Acceptance was 24 of 24 per arm. Hints fired on 4 of 32 turns and changed no rounds.

Do not read that as a verdict on `consult` or on decision models in general. It says that one design cost time and bought nothing visible on that sample.

## Why it matters

A main model is slow and expensive for the small judgments an agent makes constantly: which file to open, whether a web page is trying to instruct it, whether a queued message means stop.

The judge screen numbers show a decision can return in about a tenth of a verdict's time. If small decisions like these can steer the larger model, long agent work gets cheaper and safer.

The clock is a poor measure of that. A decision that adds a second and saves a wrong branch is a win that total time can hide, and a saved second that leads the agent astray is a loss. That is why the direction below is to evaluate on trajectories.

## Directions to work on

### Evaluate on trajectories

Define what a better path means and measure it per episode: rounds, tool calls, files read and then never used, repeated failed commands, cost, and whether the result was accepted. Clio Coder journals each decision without its content, so the outcome, latency, route, and answering build can be set against the rest of the run.

Agents did not reach for `consult`, so a first result may be about adoption: what tool description or prompting makes an agent use it when it would help, and whether forcing the call helps at all.

### Form better questions

`consult` asks yes-or-no, pick, or rate questions over a small state, and it filters lists against one criterion.

Each engine declares what it can carry, and a question that does not fit abstains instead of being cut down. Open work includes what to put in a digest so that behavior queries improve, how to phrase criteria, and which of an agent's choices are worth asking about.

### Bring a model, and one day train one

You can bring a model today. A server that answers `POST /v1/systemone` becomes a route, and a named capability profile says how its numbers are read. Profiles make no accuracy claim, and there are no fitted thresholds, so a comparison across engines would be new evidence.

Training is an open research direction with no plan or timeline. There is no training data: the decision dataset from earlier releases was removed, and today's journal keeps decision records without content. Building an opt-in dataset is part of the work, including what consent it needs, what to redact, and what counts as a correct label.

## Use Clio Coder on it today

You need a working chat model, since System One never replaces it, and a route to name. Off is the default and sends nothing.

### Name a route

```sh
clio-coder systemone use jev
clio-coder systemone status
clio-coder systemone check jev --live
```

`status` says what each route reaches and sends. `check --live` sends one content-free decision and reports the build that answered, which shows the route works and says nothing about its quality. A choice takes effect on the next start. For one headless run, pass `--systemone`:

```sh
clio-coder run --systemone jev "<task>"
clio-coder run --systemone off "<task>"
```

### Choose what answers

- `jev` is a hosted engine that needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and returns real probabilities.
- A declared engine is a decision server you run, with a named profile.
- `memory`, `main`, or a chat target answer with one label per question. They have no real probabilities, so a filter match has no score and they never drive the judge screen.

A hosted route receives file digests and heads, chunks of results, web and MCP result text, and queued messages. Redaction is best effort. Use a route you run yourself when that matters.

### Read what happened

```sh
clio-coder telemetry timeline <session-id>
clio-coder telemetry inspect <session-id> --json
```

The timeline includes each System One decision. Use `clio-coder telemetry inspect --run <run-id>` for a dispatched or headless run.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, the result is useful whichever way it comes out.

**Score the filter on a repository you know.** This extends the measurements above to new code, adds precision, and needs an afternoon.

### Write the labels before you run anything

Pick a repository you know well. Write 12 queries, six about what a file is for and six about what a file does in its body. For each query, list by hand the files that should match.

### Run each query through `consult`

Ask for the filter form directly, one query per headless run, so the agent's choice not to call the tool does not get in the way:

```sh
clio-coder run --systemone jev "Call consult with a files filter over src/**. Criterion: <query>. Use limit 32. Report the matches and do nothing else."
```

One filter carries at most 256 items and returns at most 32 matches, so scope `paths` to fit and keep each hand-labelled list shorter than that.

### Score it

For each query, compute recall and precision against your labels, separately for the two query types. Note `carried.partial` and which items carried a digest or a head.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the repository's language and size, the build `check --live` reported, your query types, and the scores. Include your sample size and leave out anything private.

Needs: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for Jev, or your own decision server. A label route can also run this, though it returns no scores, so a comparison with Jev is a second result.

A natural second experiment, also proposed and not yet run, is a small paired on/off study: the same task and the same model, repeated with `--systemone jev` and `--systemone off`, scored on the trajectory measures above. It needs tasks whose result can be accepted or rejected mechanically, and enough repeats to report an interval.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- System One is not a safety net. The deterministic safety rules and the judge decide, the screen can only tighten, and no use removes a confirmation.
- A filter miss is not proof, especially when `carried.partial` is above zero.
- Clio Coder ships a client for these wires and no inference server.

**Next steps**

- [The full System One guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/docs/guide/system-one.md)
- [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/sealed-run-records.html)
- [Let Clio Coder work without watching every call](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)

---

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/sealed-run-records.html

# Can an agent run be a scientific record?

> What a sealed run record proves and what it cannot, how far repeated runs differ, and a first experiment to measure that spread with Clio Coder.

What would it take to treat an agent run as a scientific record that someone else can check? Clio Coder already writes a sealed record of each run. Nobody has yet studied what those records can support as evidence, how much two runs of one task differ, or what a reader in another lab would still need.

**Open question, described for v0.6.8**

The records and commands on this page have shipped. The research use of them is new. No reproducibility study exists yet, so this page has no outcome numbers, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Repeatability.** Given the same task, repository, and model, how far apart are the results of repeated runs, and which recorded facts explain the difference?
- **Sufficiency.** What must a shared record contain before an outside reader can judge a claim about a run without re-running it?
- **Method.** Can sealed records carry a controlled comparison between agent configurations well enough to publish?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from the source at this version. They are not study results.

A finished run writes its settlement, its result object, and an assessment, then seals them. A seal records a SHA-256 hash chain over the journal, plus the size and hash of every journal segment and stored object. `clio-coder telemetry verify` checks all of that using only the scope's own files, so it works on any machine.

**What a seal shows.** The record's files match their manifest and the chain is intact, so damage and partial edits are caught.

**What a seal does not show.** The chain is unkeyed and carries no signature, so someone with the files could write a consistent new record, and a seal cannot say who produced it. Verification also runs nothing. A verified seal says the record is intact, and leaves open whether the agent's work was correct or would come out the same again.

Other parts of the design matter to a researcher:

- Unknowns stay unknown. A missing token count reads as not recorded instead of zero, and a dropped or refused record leaves a gap record behind.
- An assessment keeps trust states separately, including whether a run's claims were grounded in commands that actually ran.
- Sharing has three profiles. `content-free` is the default, `structural` adds structure such as prompt and tool-schema manifests, and `research` adds content captured under consent.
- A share re-applies secret redaction, and below `research` it keeps only allowlisted fields and anonymizes identities. Redaction is best effort.

## Why it matters

A success rate and a description of the setup leave a reader unable to see what an agent did, what it cost, or which results were lost along the way. A record format that keeps those facts, and says plainly when one is missing, could raise the standard of evidence.

Every other page in this section depends on the answer. A study of decision models, memory, or compaction is only as good as the records behind it, and the variance between repeated runs sets how many episodes such a study needs.

## Directions to work on

**Measure run-to-run variance.** Model output varies, and so does what the agent chooses to read. A baseline spread for rounds, cost, and accepted results on a few task types would give every later study its sample size.

**Decide what provenance needs.** An unkeyed chain suits integrity on your own machine. A shared claim may need more, such as a signature or a published digest. Designing that, and testing whether it is worth its cost, is open work.

**Test what a reader can conclude.** Give someone a `content-free` archive and a claim. Find out which claims they can check, which need `structural` or `research`, and what is still missing.

**Build the analysis layer.** Clio Coder exposes JSON reads over its journals, and it has no comparison tool. A small script that folds two sets of runs into a paired table would help every study here.

## Use Clio Coder on it today

### Run a task and read its record

```sh
clio-coder run --agent <agent-id> --json "<task>"
clio-coder telemetry inspect --run <run-id> --json
clio-coder telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json
```

`clio-coder agents` lists the agents. For a supported local or OpenAI-compatible runtime, `--temperature` sets the sampler for one run. The JSON stream ends with a result frame, and the run has its own scope.

### Verify it

```sh
clio-coder telemetry verify --run <run-id>
clio-coder fleet verify <run-id> --json
```

`telemetry verify` reports the seal. `fleet verify` also reads the settlement and reports the mismatch kind when a seal fails.

### Share it

```sh
clio-coder telemetry share --run <run-id> --profile content-free --dry-run
clio-coder telemetry share --run <run-id> --profile content-free --out run.tar.gz
clio-coder telemetry verify run.tar.gz
```

Nothing is uploaded. Read the `--dry-run` output before you send an archive to anyone. On another machine, `clio-coder telemetry import run.tar.gz` verifies the archive and places it for reading.

### Capture more, deliberately

```sh
clio-coder telemetry consent --workspace <dir>
```

Set `telemetry.mode: research` and turn on the `telemetry.research` flags you need. Content capture also needs consent for that workspace. Research capture is capped at 256 MiB per session, and a refusal leaves a gap record.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, the spread you measure is the first baseline this project has.

**Measure the spread of one small task.**

### Fix the setup

Choose a small repository with a test suite, and a task whose result those tests can accept or reject. Commit the starting state. Fix the model, route, and Clio Coder version, and write them down.

### Run it ten times

Run the task ten times, each from a clean checkout of the same commit. Pass `--temperature 0` as well if your route supports it, then repeat the set without it if you have the budget.

### Fold the records

For each run, read `telemetry inspect --run <run-id> --json` and `telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json`. Tabulate tool calls, tokens, cost, duration, stop reason, and whether the tests accepted the result. Report the median and the range.

### Check it from outside

Share two runs with `--profile content-free`, then give the archives and your table to a colleague on another machine. Record what they could verify and what they had to take on trust.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the setup, the table, and your colleague's notes. Ten runs is a small sample, so say so.

Needs: any chat route and a repository with tests. A local model server avoids API keys and spend. A second machine is only needed for the last step.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- A seal shows integrity of the record. It is not proof of correctness, authorship, or repeatability.
- Share profiles reduce what leaves your machine, and redaction is best effort, so read what you are about to share.
- Publish numbers and methods. Do not attach another person's session content without their agreement.

**Next steps**

- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/system-one-decisions.html)
- [All open questions](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/proactive-memory.html

# Does agent memory change outcomes?

> Whether lessons change what an agent does, whether self-approval is safe, and a first experiment on one repeated mistake.

Does memory make an agent better at the next task, or does it only add text to a prompt? Clio Coder has a working memory system with an approval gate, and it can also approve some of its own lessons. Nobody has yet measured whether any of this changes outcomes.

**Open question, described for v0.6.8**

Proactive memory has shipped and is on by default. This page has no outcome numbers because none exist yet, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Effect.** With a relevant lesson available, does an agent avoid a mistake it would otherwise repeat, at what model cost?
- **Trust.** Is the rule that lets a repository lesson approve itself safe, and how often does it approve something wrong?
- **Timing.** When should a reminder appear so that an agent acts on it without being distracted by it?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design at this version. They are not study results.

The design follows Wu et al., *Remember When It Matters: Proactive Memory Agent for Long-Horizon Agents* (2026), adapted to Clio Coder. A session keeps bounded banks of knowledge, attempts, and diagnoses. A rules tier makes no model calls. A model tier uses the memory route, or the chat route when no memory route is set, so a default install spends model calls on memory.

Durable lessons are separate from those banks, and only eligible approved records reach a prompt. A person can approve any record.

Repository knowledge from a task-bank entry can also receive automatic approval once one session records that the lesson held, with no contradiction or recorded regression. It waits for a person if another approved or rejected lesson already carries the same command as evidence.

Clio Coder records two useful observations about an approved lesson: `delivered` when its reminder was submitted, and `held` when the recommended command then succeeds exactly. A held lesson did not necessarily cause that success, and the agent might have run the command anyway. That gap is the research problem in one sentence.

## Why it matters

Long agent work fails in repetitive ways: the same wrong command, the same forgotten convention, the same dead end after a reset.

Memory is the obvious fix, and also an easy way to pay for tokens that do nothing, or to teach an agent something false that then persists across sessions. Evidence here would tell users when to leave it on and developers what to cut.

## Directions to work on

**Measure counterfactual effect.** Compare paired sessions on seeded tasks with memory on and off, and with a lesson present and absent. Count repeated failures, rounds, and cost, including memory's own calls.

**Audit the approval gate.** Collect automatically approved lessons from real repositories and have a person grade them. A false-approval rate, even from a small sample, would be new evidence about whether one held session is enough.

**Study reminder timing.** Reminders can land at tool-batch boundaries, at turn end, or on the next prompt. Cadence is configurable, so whether frequent reminders help or distract can be tested.

**Compare memory routes.** A small local model and the main chat model may produce very different lessons at very different costs.

## Use Clio Coder on it today

### Look at what memory is doing

Open `/memory` in the terminal. Its tabs are **Lessons**, **This task**, **Review**, and **Diagnostics**. In **Review**, `a` approves a proposal and `x` rejects it. From the shell, `clio-coder memory` lists, approves, rejects, and prunes durable records.

### Control the conditions

In `/settings`, **Memory connection** and **Memory model** choose the route. **Proactive memory** turns the whole system off, or set `context.memory.enabled: false` in project settings for one arm of a study. Cost appears in `/usage` and `clio-coder usage report`.

### Capture more when you need it

```sh
clio-coder telemetry consent --workspace <dir>
```

With `telemetry.mode: research`, consent for that workspace, and `telemetry.research.content` on, Clio Coder also records memory traces in the session's journal. This stores redacted content, so use a repository you may study.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. A result of no effect would be just as useful.

**Does one approved lesson stop a repeated mistake?**

### Seed a trap

Make a small repository where the obvious test command fails and a documented, less obvious one succeeds. Put the working command somewhere an agent must look for it. Commit that state.

### Teach it once

Run one session that hits the trap and finds the way through. Check `/memory`, and approve a lesson that names the working command. If none is proposed, write that down, since it is itself a finding.

### Run paired arms

From fresh checkouts, run the same new task five times with the lesson available and five times with `context.memory.enabled: false`. Keep the model and version fixed.

### Score it

For each session, count failed attempts of the obvious command, tool calls, and total cost from `clio-coder telemetry cost <session-id> --json`. Report the numbers for each arm and say the sample is small.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the setup, the table, and the lesson's text.

Needs: any chat route and a repository you can publish or describe. A local model server avoids keys and spend. Durable memory lives in your own state directory, so set `CLIO_CODER_HOME` to a separate directory for the study and keep your real lessons out of it.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- `held` is an evidence-gate input and is not proof of a general claim.
- Stored memory is not fine-tuning of the underlying model.
- A background model never writes directly to the system prompt.

**Next steps**

- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [Proactive memory guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/proactive-memory.html)
- [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/sealed-run-records.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/context-and-retrieval.html

# What does an agent lose when its context is reduced?

> Fidelity of summaries, the cost of reduction, and search by meaning, with a first experiment that counts how many planted facts survive.

When an agent's conversation is reduced to fit a model's window, what gets lost, and what does that loss cost later? Clio Coder has several ways to reduce context and an optional index for finding things by meaning. It measures size and cost carefully. It does not yet measure whether the agent still knows what it needs.

**Open question, described for v0.6.8**

Compaction has shipped and is on by default. Semantic context is a beta feature that is off by default. This page has no fidelity numbers because none exist yet, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Fidelity.** Which facts survive a summary, and which kinds are most often dropped: constraints, decisions, file paths, or test results?
- **Policy.** When should a system evict old material, summarize it, or keep it, given what each choice does to the model's cache and to the next request's cost?
- **Retrieval.** Does search by meaning help an agent find the right material, compared with the `grep` and code map it already has?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design at this version. They are not study results.

Automatic reduction normally starts at 80% of the effective window, or earlier at a 200,000-token ceiling. Working-set eviction runs first, then summarization if that is not enough. The default eviction policy is `structural-v2`. Summaries follow a fixed checkpoint shape: goal, constraints and preferences, progress, key decisions, next steps, and critical context.

Clio Coder records whether a reduction gained anything. A summary that would not shrink the context is discarded, its cost stays in the totals, and an identical later automatic request makes no call. The journals also separate what a call read from cache and what it had to send again, so the cost side can be measured precisely.

The quality side has no measure. A checkpoint can be small, valid, and missing the one constraint that matters, and nothing would notice.

Semantic context can index code maps, wiki pages, approved memory, evidence, and registered folders with a local embedding model. Its `--qualify` check confirms that a route accepts requests and returns vectors of the right shape. It does not check retrieval quality.

## Why it matters

Long tasks now routinely outlive a model's window. A summary is a lossy step in the middle of every one of them, and its failures look like the model being forgetful or careless later on. A fidelity benchmark would let anyone compare summarizers, prompts, and policies with something better than impressions.

Cost matters too. A reduction can also break the model's cache, so the cheapest-looking choice in the moment can be expensive over the following turns.

## Directions to work on

**Build a fidelity benchmark.** Plant facts of known types in a real session, reduce it, then probe. Open sets of sessions and probes would be useful to other agent projects as well.

**Compare summarizers and instructions.** `context.compaction.model` can name a smaller model, and `/context compact <what to keep>` directs a summary. Does a cheap model lose more, and does stating what to keep actually help?

**Compare policies on total cost.** Vary `context.compaction.threshold`, `context.compaction.maxTokens`, and the working-set policy, then measure cost and cache behavior over a whole task.

**Evaluate retrieval on real questions.** Label a set of questions about a repository, then compare semantic search with `grep` and the code map on recall and on how many tool calls the agent spends.

## Use Clio Coder on it today

### Inspect and reduce

Open `/context` for usage, the output reserve, headroom, and any pending handoff. Then reduce with a stated purpose:

```text
/context compact Keep the objective, decisions, changed files, test results, and remaining work.
```

### Read the cost

```sh
clio-coder telemetry cache <session-id> --json
clio-coder telemetry cost <session-id> --json
clio-coder telemetry timeline <session-id> --json
```

### Try semantic search

```sh
clio-coder semantic configure --help
clio-coder semantic refresh
clio-coder semantic search "Which run produced the delayed oscillation?" --limit 5
```

This needs a local embedding route. The [semantic context tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/semantic-context-and-recordings.html) walks through setup.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. Its materials would become the start of a shared benchmark.

**How many planted facts survive one summary?**

### Plant the facts

Write 20 short facts, five each of four types: a constraint, a decision with its reason, a specific file path, and a test result. State them to the agent across the first part of a real coding session, then keep working until the session holds plenty of other material.

### Reduce the same session two ways

Use `/fork` to branch the session before reducing. Run `/context compact` with no instructions on one branch, and with instructions naming what to keep on the other.

### Probe

Ask each branch the same 20 questions, one per fact, and tell it not to open any file. Score each answer as correct, wrong, or missing, and have someone else grade a sample.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the survival rate by fact type for each branch, the model used, and the session size before and after. One session is an anecdote, so say so, and repeat it if you can.

Needs: any chat route, and a session long enough to reduce. A local model server avoids keys. Leave the session content out of what you publish unless you may share it.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- A probe measures recall on request. An agent may still fail to apply a fact it can recite.
- Similarity finds candidates. It is not proof of a result.
- Telling a model not to open files limits what it does only as far as it follows that instruction, so check the tool calls.

**Next steps**

- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [Context continuity guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/context-continuity.html)
- [Search your project by meaning and record worker runs](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/semantic-context-and-recordings.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/fleets-and-local-models.html

# When do several agents or small models pay off?

> Compete, council, heterogeneous fleets and local models, with no comparative numbers yet and a first experiment on one seeded bug.

When is it worth running several agents on one problem, and how small a model can still do useful work? Clio Coder can run workers across local and remote machines, have candidates compete, and convene a council of models. These are shipped controls. We have no comparative numbers on when any of them pays off.

**Open question, described for v0.6.8**

The fleet features on this page have shipped. This page has no comparative results because none exist yet, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Multi-agent value.** Per dollar and per hour, when does compete or council beat one agent on the same task?
- **Local capability.** Which coding tasks can a model on one workstation finish, and where does it fail?
- **Heterogeneous fleets.** Does a mix of a strong planner and small workers beat a uniform fleet of either?
- **Other model families.** Do diffusion language models hold up on long agentic work?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design at this version. They are not study results.

Compete runs 2 to 4 candidates in scratch worktrees with a read-only judge. A council runs two to five read-only members on the same task, with optional vote or judge synthesis. A review gate adds a read-only reviewer and a bounded revise loop. Workers can be routed per agent or per call, on the local machine or on SSH nodes.

Each run is sealed with its route, tokens, cost, and assessment, so a comparison can be built from records.

Clio Coder reads local servers such as LM Studio, Ollama, and llama.cpp, and asks each for its real serving window where it can. Inception's Mercury diffusion models are available for chat and workers. They are less tested on long agentic work than the models most people use.

What is missing is any measurement across these options. A sealed record shows what one run did, which leaves open whether a different arrangement would have done better.

## Why it matters

Running four agents costs roughly four times as much, and it is not obvious what that buys. Local models matter for a different reason: some groups cannot send their code or data to a cloud provider, and they need to know what a workstation can really do before they build on it.

## Directions to work on

**Price multi-agent modes.** Take tasks with mechanical acceptance, then compare one agent, a 2-candidate compete, and a council on acceptance, cost, and time.

**Map the local frontier.** Run a graded set of tasks against a few local models. Report where tool calling, long context, and multi-file edits each break down.

**Test placement.** Try a strong orchestrator with small local workers, and the reverse. `fleet.concurrency`, worker profiles, and per-call pins give the controls.

**Try diffusion models on agent work.** Compare Mercury with a token-by-token model of similar speed or price on the same tasks.

## Use Clio Coder on it today

### Connect a local model

Run `clio-coder configure` and choose **Connect by endpoint** for a local server. LM Studio commonly serves at `http://localhost:1234`, and Ollama at `http://localhost:11434`. Choose a model that supports tool calling. The [local model tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/run-on-a-local-model.html) walks through it.

### Run a single worker with a record

```sh
clio-coder run --agent <agent-id> --target <target-id> --json "<task>"
clio-coder telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json
```

`--target` and `--model` override the route for one run, so one script can sweep several models.

### Use the multi-agent shapes

In a session, ask the agent to dispatch your task in compete mode with two candidates. For a council, use `/council`:

```text
/council --synthesis judge <task>
```

Rosters are set in settings. `clio-coder fleet status --json` lists runs, and `clio-coder doctor` reports readiness.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. Even a result on one bug gives the next person a method to improve.

**One seeded bug: is a 2-candidate compete worth it on a local model?**

### Prepare the task

Take a small repository with a good test suite and introduce one bug that makes a test fail. Commit that state, and write down the bug so you can grade results.

### Run both arms

From fresh checkouts, run a single agent five times and a 2-candidate compete five times, with the same model and version.

### Score it

Record for each trial whether the suite passes with the original tests unchanged, total tokens from the run records, and elapsed time. Local models have no bill, so report tokens and time.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the model, the hardware, the table, and your sample size.

Needs: one machine that can run a tool-calling model through a local server. A GPU helps but is not required for a small model. No keys. Extra SSH nodes are optional.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- One bug in one repository does not generalize, so report it as what it is.
- Worker slots limit concurrency. They are not an allocation, and a login node is not a compute node.
- A cloud model sends its input to that provider, including from a remote node.

**Next steps**

- [Choose a model for your project](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [Fleet guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Diffusion models in the terminal](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/diffusion-models.html)

Source: https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html

# What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?

> Pre-registered checks, validated modernization and scheduler use on scientific code, with a first experiment on catching a numerical error.

What evidence would convince a domain scientist that a change made by an agent is correct? Scientific code has checks most software lacks, such as conservation laws, reference solutions, and published results.

It also has its own hazards, including schedulers, shared allocations, and results that look plausible while being wrong. Clio Coder has shipped tools for this work. Nobody has yet studied how far they go.

**Open question, described for v0.6.8**

The skills and integrations on this page have shipped. This page has no study results because none exist yet, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. The team, students, and outside researchers are welcome, especially people who own real scientific codes.

## The question

- **Trust.** What must an agent produce so that a domain expert accepts a numerical change, and does an external reference or a pre-registered check actually catch wrong results?
- **Modernization.** Can an agent port or rewrite established scientific software in stages, with each stage independently validated, at acceptable cost?
- **Cluster work.** Can an agent use a scheduler responsibly, and what does it waste when it does not?

## What is known so far

These are facts about what ships at this version. They are not study results.

The library has research skills. `experiment-protocol` pre-registers a performance study, numerical comparison, sweep, or benchmark, locking thresholds, tolerances, environment pins, and verdict conditions before any measurement. `scientific-modernization` ports or rewrites scientific software in independently validated stages against an external scientific oracle.

`scientific-debugging`, `slurm-jobs`, and `arxiv-literature` are also there, and the `materio` plugin supports materials-science research.

For clusters, Clio Coder installs without root on a login node, and it reaches Slurm through the clio-kit MCP server, with each job action going through your approval. Clio Coder does not submit its own workers through a scheduler.

The one worked example is [a temperature-calibration change](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html), recorded from a real session with seven tests. It is a demonstration on a small task. No study covers real solvers, a domain expert's judgment, or how often an oracle catches an agent's error.

## Why it matters

A wrong numerical result can look fine and travel into a paper. If agents are going to touch scientific code, the field needs methods that make their errors visible, and evidence about which methods work. Some research groups also hold old codes that few people can maintain, so careful, validated modernization could be valuable if it can be trusted.

## Directions to work on

**Test the oracle.** Inject known errors into a scientific kernel and find out how often a pre-registered check catches them, and how often an agent talks its way around one.

**Run a real modernization.** Take a small code with reference output through `scientific-modernization`, and report stages, costs, failures, and what the maintainer thought of the result.

**Measure scheduler behavior.** Using a small allocation, record what an agent submits, how often it resubmits, and how much of the allocation produces useful output.

**Study expert acceptance.** Show domain scientists an agent's change with and without its evidence, and ask what they would accept and why.

## Use Clio Coder on it today

### Install a research skill

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:experiment-protocol --project --dry-run
clio-coder library install skill:experiment-protocol --project
```

Then call it in a session:

```text
/skill experiment-protocol Compare my solver against the reference output. Define the tolerances before running anything.
```

### Add Slurm when you need it

Install clio-kit on a host where `sbatch` reaches your cluster, declare its server in `mcp.yaml`, and install the skill. The [Slurm guide](https://coder.iowarp.ai/docs/guide/slurm.html) gives the exact file.

```sh
clio-coder library install skill:slurm-jobs --project
```

The [pre-registration tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/pre-register-a-benchmark.html) and the [Slurm tutorial](https://coder.iowarp.ai/tutorials/submit-a-slurm-job.html) walk through both.

### Keep the record

Headless runs and dispatched workers are sealed, so a study can cite and share them. [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://coder.iowarp.ai/research/sealed-run-records.html) covers what that does and does not show.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. A kernel with published reference output is a good place to begin.

**Can a pre-registered check catch an agent's numerical error?**

### Choose a kernel

Pick a small numerical routine with reference output you trust, from your field if possible. Put it in a repository with its reference data.

### Pre-register

Use `experiment-protocol` to lock the tolerances and verdict conditions, and commit them before any change is made.

### Ask for a port

Ask the agent to port or refactor the kernel, and run the check. Record the verdict, the cost, and whether the agent edited anything it should not have.

### Inject an error

Separately, introduce a subtle error, such as a changed constant or a lost precision step, then ask the agent to review the code and run the check. Record whether it was caught, and by what.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the kernel, the tolerances, the verdicts, and what a person in the field made of the result.

Needs: a laptop and any chat route for everything above. A local model server avoids sending code to a provider. A cluster account is needed only for scheduler work.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/iowarp/clio-coder/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- A passing check shows only what that check tests. Choose it with someone who knows the science.
- Your site's access rules, allocation limits, and data policies apply to anything an agent does there.
- Do not publish data or code you may not share.
